name: AWS Operational Readiness Review
description: Operational Readiness Review (ORR) custom lens 2.0.1 for the AWS Well-Architected Tool, informed by the AWS Operational Readiness Reviews whitepaper and Well-Architected best practice OPS07-BP02. High risk means launch-blocking unless remediated or formally accepted in writing by the accountable owner. Medium means fix on a plan. This lens is guidance. It is not an AWS certification, compliance attestation, audit or SLA. Completing it does not mean AWS has reviewed your workload, and it does not change the AWS shared responsibility model. Numeric targets are this lens's suggestions. Provided as is under the MIT-0 license. Source and updates: https://github.com/awslabs/operational-readiness-review-custom-war-lens

questions.title: Current Well-Architected review with high risks dispositioned
questions.description: Maximum risk: High (launch-blocking unless remediated or formally accepted). Category: Readiness governance. Does the workload have a current AWS Well-Architected Framework review whose high-risk issues are all remediated, owned or formally accepted, so that this ORR can focus on launch-blocking operational risk? Evidence to collect: the Well-Architected review report with its date and the lenses applied. The milestone saved at the review. The date of the last major architecture change. The open high-risk issues with owner role, target date or risk-register reference.

helpfulResource.displayText: The review process (AWS Well-Architected Framework)

choices.title: A Well-Architected Framework review was completed in the last 12 months and after the last major architecture change

helpfulResource.displayText: Good looks like: The workload has a Framework review covering all six pillars, recorded in the AWS Well-Architected Tool or an equivalent documented review, dated within the last 12 months and after the last major architecture change. It was answered by people who own the current design, a milestone was saved at the end so later reviews can be compared with it, and the next review date is scheduled. Partition notes: The AWS Well-Architected Tool is available in AWS GovCloud (US) as of 2026-10-05, without Profiles or the Jira connector. Account IDs associated with a workload, the workload name, milestone names and the review owner may leave the AWS GovCloud (US) Regions in normal operation, so keep export-controlled and sensitive data out of those fields.

improvementPlan.displayText: Run or refresh the Framework review in the AWS Well-Architected Tool with the people who own the design, answer every question against the architecture as it is today, save a milestone, and schedule the next review for 12 months later or the next major architecture change, whichever comes first. Attach the review date and milestone name to the ORR evidence.

content.displayText: Milestones in the AWS Well-Architected Tool

choices.title: Every open high-risk issue from that review is remediated, owned with a target date, or formally accepted

helpfulResource.displayText: Good looks like: Each high-risk issue still open in the review has a recorded disposition: remediated, with the answer updated; owned, with an owner role and a target date in the improvement plan or backlog; or formally accepted in writing by the accountable owner, with a reason and an expiry date. No high-risk issue is left undecided at launch. Acceptances live in your risk register and the review notes carry only a reference, for example EXC:<register-id> exp:YYYY-MM-DD role:<approver-role>, never names.

improvementPlan.displayText: Export the open high-risk issues from the improvement plan, give each one an owner role and a target date in your backlog, fix those that are launch-blocking for this workload, and take any you will not fix to the accountable owner for written acceptance with an expiry date. Review the list again at each milestone and before the launch decision.

content.displayText: OPS01-BP06 Evaluate tradeoffs while managing benefits and risks (AWS Well-Architected)

choices.title: Applicable AWS lenses (for example Government, Serverless Applications, Generative AI) were applied, or none apply

helpfulResource.displayText: Good looks like: The review applied every AWS lens that fits the workload's technology or industry, for example the Government, Serverless Applications or Generative AI lens from the Lens Catalog, or recorded why none applies. High-risk issues from those lenses are dispositioned the same way as Framework high-risk issues.

improvementPlan.displayText: Compare the Lens Catalog, and the AWS lenses distributed as custom lens files, with the workload's technology and industry. Add the relevant lenses to the workload, answer them before the launch decision, and disposition their high-risk issues.

questions.title: System model: diagrams, critical journeys and failure modes
questions.description: Maximum risk: Medium (not launch-blocking, remediate on a plan). Category: Defense against dependencies. Does the team share a current model of how the workload works and how each component and dependency can fail, with a detection signal and a mitigation for each significant failure mode? Evidence to collect: current architecture and data-flow diagrams. The table of critical journeys and APIs with the components and dependencies each one uses. The failure mode analysis and its last review date. The mapping from failure modes to alarms, runbooks and design controls.

helpfulResource.displayText: Resilience analysis framework (AWS Prescriptive Guidance)

choices.title: Current architecture and data-flow diagrams map each critical user journey and API to the components and dependencies it uses

helpfulResource.displayText: Good looks like: Diagrams stored with the code or in a shared, versioned location show components, AWS accounts, Regions and Availability Zones, data stores, network paths, and every internal and external dependency. A table lists each critical user journey and each customer-facing API, public or private, what it does, and the components and dependencies it touches. Both were updated in or after the last major change. Platform notes: Serverless and event-driven workloads: include event sources, queues, streams, schedules and other asynchronous paths, which diagrams often omit. Containers: include cluster add-ons, service discovery and the image registry. EC2: include AMI sources, bootstrap dependencies and load balancer health checks.

improvementPlan.displayText: Draw the current architecture and data flows from your infrastructure as code and from observed traffic, list the critical journeys and APIs with the dependencies each one uses, store both with the code, and update them in the same change that alters the architecture.

choices.title: A failure mode analysis of every component and dependency is documented and reviewed yearly or after major changes

helpfulResource.displayText: Good looks like: A failure mode analysis lists, for every component and dependency, its hard and soft failure modes (for example unavailable, slow, erroring, throttling or returning bad data) with the service impact and the customer impact of each. It covers loss of the largest blast-radius unit the workload uses, such as a cell, an Availability Zone or a Region, and was reviewed in the last 12 months or after the last major change.

improvementPlan.displayText: Run a structured analysis, for example with the resilience analysis framework or Failure Mode and Effects Analysis (FMEA): walk each component and dependency through each failure category, record the impact and the protections that already exist, rank the gaps, and schedule a review every 12 months and after major changes.

choices.title: Each significant failure mode maps to an alarm or other detection signal

helpfulResource.displayText: Good looks like: For each significant failure mode, the analysis names the alarm, canary or other signal that detects it and how quickly. Failure modes that nothing detects are listed as gaps with an owner and a date, and each mapping was checked against a past incident or an injected fault.

improvementPlan.displayText: Add a detection column to the failure mode analysis, map each failure mode to an existing alarm or canary, create alarms for the gaps, and confirm each mapping by injecting the failure in a test environment or by replaying a past incident.

choices.title: Each significant failure mode has a documented mitigation: a design control, automation or a runbook

helpfulResource.displayText: Good looks like: Each significant failure mode has a documented mitigation: a design control (for example redundancy, a timeout or a degraded mode), an automated response, or a runbook with tested steps. Failure modes the team chose not to mitigate are recorded with the reason and the accountable owner. Reader note: This page links an article that uses AWS CloudTrail Lake, which is closed to new customers; any runbook format or tool meets this practice.

improvementPlan.displayText: Add a mitigation column, link each failure mode to the control, automation or runbook that handles it, write runbooks for the gaps, and put design changes for failure modes with high customer impact and no mitigation on the backlog with an owner and a date.

questions.title: Regional isolation and data-plane-only recovery
questions.description: Maximum risk: High (launch-blocking unless remediated or formally accepted). Category: Blast radius containment. Do steady state and recovery avoid depending on control planes, other Regions, or shared resources that can fail at the same time as the failure you are recovering from? Evidence to collect: the failover and recovery runbooks with each API call classified as control plane or data plane. The list of cross-Region and global-service dependencies on the critical path. Resources shared across Availability Zones, cells or Regions. The account structure and organization policies. The last failover test record.

helpfulResource.displayText: REL11-BP04 Data plane recovery (AWS Well-Architected)

choices.title: Failover uses data-plane actions on pre-provisioned resources, and no recovery step creates resources in the impaired location

helpfulResource.displayText: Good looks like: Every failover step moves traffic to, or changes state on, resources that already exist and are sized for the load (for example Route 53 health-check failover records or an ARC zonal shift), with no launches, resource changes, or IAM or DNS edits through a control plane. Under an approved backup-and-restore or pilot-light strategy, steps that create or scale resources run only in the recovery Region or account, need neither the impaired Region nor a global service control plane, fit inside RTO, and were proven in the last DR test. Capacity to survive losing an Availability Zone is scored in event_resilience_recoveries (az_static_capacity). Platform notes: Serverless: size concurrency and quotas in the recovery location ahead of time, and never deploy functions or stacks into the impaired Region during recovery. Partition notes: ARC routing control is not available in AWS GovCloud (US) as of 2026-10-05; Route 53 failover routing and ARC zonal shift are available there (verify per Region).

improvementPlan.displayText: List every action in the failover and recovery runbooks and classify each API call as control plane or data plane. Replace control-plane steps with pre-provisioned resources and data-plane mechanisms such as Route 53 health checks or ARC zonal shift, pre-scale or reserve the capacity the remaining locations need, and prove the plan in a failover test that does not use the replaced control-plane actions.

content.displayText: Static stability using Availability Zones (Amazon Builders' Library)
REL11-BP05 Use static stability to prevent bimodal behavior (AWS Well-Architected)

Related AWS Post-Event Summary (Oct 2025): existing EC2 instances remained healthy while new instance launches failed for hours, so recover with capacity that is already running and with data-plane actions rather than by launching or modifying resources.
Configuring DNS failover (Amazon Route 53)
Zonal shift in Amazon Application Recovery Controller (ARC)

choices.title: The critical path and recovery steps have no runtime dependency on another Region or on a global service's control plane

helpfulResource.displayText: Good looks like: Requests and recovery steps make no runtime call that needs another Region or a global service's control plane, which the AWS Fault Isolation Boundaries whitepaper places in a single Region (for example IAM, Route 53 public DNS and CloudFront). Credentials come from Regional AWS STS endpoints, configuration and secrets are replicated or cached in the Region, and global-service changes are never a recovery step. Failing over to a recovery Region meets this, as long as the steps run in the recovery Region and need nothing from the impaired one. Platform notes: Some AWS SDKs and CLIs default to the global AWS STS endpoint, so set the STS Regional endpoints setting to regional. Avoid synchronous cross-Region calls on the critical path. Partition notes: In AWS GovCloud (US), as of 2026-10-06, the IAM and Route 53 control planes are in AWS GovCloud (US-West), so recovery steps in AWS GovCloud (US-East) must not change IAM or Route 53 configuration, and there is no global AWS STS endpoint.

improvementPlan.displayText: Trace each critical call and each recovery step to the Region and the plane it uses. Switch clients to Regional AWS STS endpoints, replicate or cache configuration and secrets in each Region, remove calls to global-service control planes from the request path and the runbooks, and create ahead of time anything those steps used to create.

content.displayText: Manage AWS STS in an AWS Region (IAM User Guide)

choices.title: No configuration, credential or resource shared across AZs, cells or Regions can impair all of them at once

helpfulResource.displayText: Good looks like: No single configuration value, credential, certificate, data store, deployment or network component is shared by every Availability Zone, cell or Region in a way that one bad change or one failure impairs all of them. Changes to anything shared roll out one fault boundary at a time, and each location keeps running on its last known good copy if the shared source is unavailable. Platform notes: Containers: one cluster spanning Availability Zones shares its control plane and add-ons, so larger workloads may use cells or more than one cluster. Serverless: one function configuration or alias serves every Availability Zone, so stage its changes. EC2: one launch template or AMI change can reach every Availability Zone at once unless the rollout is staged.

improvementPlan.displayText: List what more than one Availability Zone, cell or Region uses (for example a shared database, a global configuration file, one certificate, or one deployment that targets everything). Split those items per fault boundary where it matters, or stage their changes one boundary at a time with automatic rollback, and keep a last known good copy in each location.

content.displayText: Minimizing correlated failures in distributed systems (Amazon Builders' Library)

choices.title: Production runs in dedicated accounts isolated from non-production, with organization guardrails on logging and Regions

helpfulResource.displayText: Good looks like: Production runs in AWS accounts used only for production, separate from development and test, and managed in AWS Organizations. Service control policies or equivalent guardrails stop anyone from turning off audit logging such as AWS CloudTrail and restrict use to approved Regions, and non-production identities and pipelines have no standing access to production.

improvementPlan.displayText: Move production resources into dedicated accounts under a production organizational unit, attach service control policies that deny disabling logging and deny unapproved Regions, and remove access paths that let non-production identities or pipelines change production.

questions.title: Timeouts, bounded retries and idempotency
questions.description: Maximum risk: High (launch-blocking unless remediated or formally accepted). Category: Defense against dependencies. How do you stop slow or failing dependencies from exhausting threads, connections and memory, and keep retries from multiplying the load on a dependency that is already struggling? Evidence to collect: the client configuration for each remote call (connect and request timeouts, retry mode, maximum attempts). The measured latency used to size each timeout. The list of layers that retry. Idempotency tokens on mutating operations. Timeout and retry metrics per dependency.

helpfulResource.displayText: REL05-BP03 Control and limit retry calls (AWS Well-Architected)

choices.title: Every remote call (AWS SDK, HTTP, database, third party, model) sets connect and request timeouts sized to observed latency

helpfulResource.displayText: Good looks like: Every remote call, including AWS SDK clients, HTTP clients, database drivers, third-party APIs and model endpoints, sets an explicit connect timeout and request or socket timeout chosen from measured latency (for example just above the p99.9 latency) rather than from library defaults. The total time across all attempts fits inside the caller's own timeout, and timeouts are counted in a metric. Platform notes: EC2 and containers: also bound connection-pool wait times and worker or thread pools. Serverless: keep downstream timeouts shorter than the Lambda function timeout and any API Gateway integration timeout, and set task timeouts in AWS Step Functions state machines.

improvementPlan.displayText: Inventory every client and driver and record its current timeouts. Measure latency per dependency, set connect and request timeouts from those measurements instead of relying on defaults, emit a timeout metric per dependency, and add a test or code review check that fails when a client is created without explicit timeouts.

choices.title: Retries, including asynchronous ones, are capped and use exponential backoff with jitter

helpfulResource.displayText: Good looks like: Every retry mechanism, including SDK retries, queue redelivery, Lambda asynchronous retries and Step Functions Retry fields, has a maximum number of attempts and waits with exponential backoff and jitter. Synchronous calls retry little, if at all, and return an error the client can act on; asynchronous work backs off for longer and then goes to a dead-letter queue that is alarmed. Platform notes: AWS SDKs: use the standard retry mode, which uses exponential backoff with jitter and a retry quota, and set maximum attempts deliberately. Serverless: set Lambda asynchronous retry attempts (0-2) and maximum event age, an Amazon SQS maxReceiveCount with a dead-letter queue, and Step Functions MaxAttempts, BackoffRate, MaxDelaySeconds and JitterStrategy.

improvementPlan.displayText: Find every retry mechanism in code, SDK configuration, queues, functions and workflows. Cap the attempts, add exponential backoff with jitter, send exhausted asynchronous work to a dead-letter queue with an alarm, and run a test with a dependency failing to confirm that retries do not multiply traffic.

content.displayText: Handling errors in AWS Step Functions workflows (Retry, BackoffRate, JitterStrategy)
Configuring error handling for Lambda asynchronous invocations
Using dead-letter queues in Amazon SQS
Retry with backoff pattern (AWS Prescriptive Guidance)

choices.title: A retry budget or circuit breaker stops retries to unhealthy or throttling dependencies, and only one layer retries

helpfulResource.displayText: Good looks like: Retries are limited as a share of traffic, with a retry budget or token bucket such as the AWS SDK retry quota, or stopped by a circuit breaker while a dependency is unhealthy or throttling, so retry traffic falls as errors rise. Only one layer in the call chain retries a given failure and the other layers fail fast. Calls to third-party APIs stay within their published rate limits.

improvementPlan.displayText: Map the call chain and remove retries from all but one layer. Enable a retry quota or budget in that layer. Add a circuit breaker only where a dependency can stay unhealthy for long periods, and test it, because circuit breakers add modal behavior. Alarm on the retry rate per dependency, and use client-side rate limiting to stay within third-party limits.

content.displayText: Related AWS Post-Event Summary (Dec 2021): rising latency and errors led to even more connection attempts and retries, which caused persistent congestion, so budget retries and stop retrying to a dependency that is already overloaded.

choices.title: Retried mutating operations are idempotent (for example client tokens), and only failed batch items are retried

helpfulResource.displayText: Good looks like: Every mutating operation that can be retried accepts an idempotency key or client token, so a retried create, payment or message has exactly one effect, and consumers of at-least-once queues and streams deduplicate. Batch consumers report only the failed items for retry instead of failing the whole batch. Platform notes: AWS APIs: Amazon EC2 and many other AWS APIs accept a client token for idempotent requests. Serverless: turn on partial batch responses (ReportBatchItemFailures) for Lambda event source mappings such as Amazon SQS.

improvementPlan.displayText: List the mutating APIs and message handlers. Add an idempotency key that the server stores with the result for a retention window, return the original result for duplicates, pass client tokens on AWS API calls that accept them, and switch batch handlers to report partial failures.

questions.title: Core journeys keep working when dependencies fail
questions.description: Maximum risk: High (launch-blocking unless remediated or formally accepted). Category: Defense against dependencies. When a non-critical dependency is slow or unavailable, do core customer journeys keep working, and does the workload recover safely when the dependency returns? Evidence to collect: the soft dependencies of each critical journey and how each is called (synchronous, asynchronous or cached). Logging and telemetry configuration, including the Amazon ECS log driver mode. The degraded behavior defined per feature. Backlog drain and admission settings. The latest fault injection results.

helpfulResource.displayText: REL05-BP01 Graceful degradation (AWS Well-Architected)

choices.title: Non-critical dependencies (logs, metrics, tracing, analytics, feature flags) cannot block or fail the request path

helpfulResource.displayText: Good looks like: Calls to logging, metrics, tracing, analytics, feature-flag and similar services are asynchronous, buffered with bounded memory, or served from a local cache, with short timeouts, so the request still completes when any of them is slow or down. The team checked each one rather than assuming it. Platform notes: Containers: since 2025-06-25 the Amazon ECS default log driver mode is non-blocking; check task definitions for mode set to blocking and the defaultLogDriverMode account setting, and with non-blocking mode size max-buffer-size and alarm on log delivery gaps, because a full buffer drops logs. Serverless: do not block a function on direct calls to CloudWatch Logs or Amazon Data Firehose. Feature flags: read them through a local cache such as AWS AppConfig Agent so the last known values keep working.

improvementPlan.displayText: List every non-critical call on the request path. Move each one off the path (asynchronous, buffered or cached with a bounded size), give it a short timeout and a defined behavior on failure, and verify by blocking each dependency in a test environment. For Amazon ECS, choose blocking or non-blocking log delivery deliberately for each container.

content.displayText: Related AWS Post-Event Summary (Jul 2024): Amazon ECS tasks whose awslogs driver used blocking mode were blocked and could not respond to health checks when logs could not be sent, while tasks using non-blocking mode ran normally, so keep logging and other soft dependencies off the request path.
Amazon ECS LogConfiguration (mode and max-buffer-size)
What is AWS AppConfig Agent? (local caching of configuration and feature flags)

choices.title: Losing a soft dependency degrades only its feature through normal code paths, not rarely exercised fallback paths

helpfulResource.displayText: Good looks like: When a soft dependency fails, only the feature that needs it degrades (for example recommendations are hidden, or cached data is shown with its age) and the rest of the journey proceeds. The degraded behavior runs through code paths used every day, such as always reading from a cache that is refreshed asynchronously, rather than a fallback that runs only during failures and is rarely exercised.

improvementPlan.displayText: For each soft dependency, agree the degraded behavior with the product owner. Implement it so the normal path already tolerates the dependency being absent, for example by using pushed or cached data on every request, remove rarely exercised fallback code where you can, and test each degraded mode.

content.displayText: AWS Fault Isolation Boundaries: Static stability

choices.title: After an outage, backlogs drain under admission control or load shedding, so queued work and retries cannot cause collapse

helpfulResource.displayText: Good looks like: After a dependency outage, queued work, client retries and reconnecting clients cannot overload the recovering system. Consumers drain backlogs at a bounded rate, fresh or high-priority work is processed first where old work has lost its value, stale work is dropped or dead-lettered, and admission control or load shedding protects the service while caches refill. Platform notes: Serverless: cap Lambda concurrency for Amazon SQS event sources with maximum concurrency, and set a maximum event age for asynchronous invocations. EC2 and containers: cap consumer concurrency and connection-pool sizes so a backlog cannot exhaust a shared database.

improvementPlan.displayText: Estimate the backlog that your longest expected dependency outage creates. Set consumer rate limits and maximum message ages, decide which work to drop, prioritize or dead-letter, and rehearse recovery by pausing a consumer or dependency under load and watching the drain.

content.displayText: Configuring scaling behavior for SQS event source mappings (maximum concurrency)

choices.title: Dependency errors, throttling, latency and unavailability were injected (for example with AWS FIS) and the behavior verified

helpfulResource.displayText: Good looks like: Experiments injected errors, throttling, added latency and full unavailability for each critical and soft dependency, in a production-like environment or in production with stop conditions, and showed that timeouts, retries, degraded modes and alarms behaved as documented. Results and fixes are recorded, and the experiments are repeated after major changes. Platform notes: AWS FIS has actions for EC2, Amazon ECS tasks, Amazon EKS pods, network disruption and Lambda (invocation errors and added delay). For third-party dependencies, inject faults in a proxy or client wrapper. Partition notes: AWS FIS is available in AWS GovCloud (US) as of 2026-10-05, but the AWS FIS experiment schedule and experiment report features are not available there, so schedule experiments from a pipeline or Amazon EventBridge Scheduler; verify per Region that the actions you need are supported.

improvementPlan.displayText: Write a hypothesis for each dependency failure mode, run experiments with stop conditions tied to alarms, start in a test environment, fix what breaks, and add the experiments to a regular schedule or a pipeline stage.

content.displayText: Use the AWS FIS aws:lambda:function actions

questions.title: Redundant private connectivity to on-premises and partner networks
questions.description: Maximum risk: High (launch-blocking unless remediated or formally accepted). Category: Defense against dependencies. If one private link, device, location or provider between AWS and your on-premises, state or partner networks fails, can the workload still reach every system on its critical path that sits behind those links? Out of scope if: the critical path has no private connection to on-premises, state or partner networks. Select the first statement and keep the evidence. Evidence to collect: a diagram of every private link on the critical path (AWS Direct Connect connections and locations, AWS Site-to-Site VPN tunnels, customer devices and providers) and the routing protocol each uses. The date and result of the last failover test. Recovery plans for on-premises identity, DNS and data dependencies.

helpfulResource.displayText: REL02-BP02 Redundant private connectivity (AWS Well-Architected)

choices.title: The critical path has no private connection to on-premises, state or partner networks

helpfulResource.displayText: Good looks like: No request, job or recovery step on the critical path depends on a system reached over AWS Direct Connect, AWS Site-to-Site VPN, a transit or partner network, or another private link. Count indirect dependencies too: DNS forwarded to on-premises resolvers, identity providers or directories hosted on premises, license servers and file transfers. Evidence to collect: route tables and transit gateway or virtual private gateway attachments showing no on-premises or partner routes on the critical path, and a data-flow diagram reviewed by the network owner. When this is selected, the other statements do not change the score.

improvementPlan.displayText: If any critical-path dependency is reached over a private link, clear this statement and answer the other statements. Recheck at every architecture change, because new integrations often add a private link.

choices.title: Each private link on the critical path has two independent, dynamically routed paths (separate locations, devices or providers)

helpfulResource.displayText: Good looks like: Every private link on the critical path has at least two paths with no shared single point of failure, and BGP moves traffic between them without manual steps. Examples: AWS Direct Connect at two Direct Connect locations, or Direct Connect plus AWS Site-to-Site VPN with tunnels on separate customer devices and, where possible, providers. Two Direct Connect locations still share the Direct Connect path into the Region (Sep 2021 Post-Event Summary), so the most critical paths also keep a VPN backup over the internet. REL02-BP02 anti-patterns: one connection, one VPN tunnel or tunnels ending in the same Availability Zone, one ISP for VPN, no dynamic routing, and VPN bandwidth too small for the backup role. Partition notes: AWS Direct Connect and AWS Site-to-Site VPN are available in AWS GovCloud (US) as of 2026-10-05. Direct Connect Partners do not support hosted connections to GovCloud account IDs, so order them with the linked standard account ID; verify per Region.

improvementPlan.displayText: Map every private link and the devices, locations and providers behind it. Add a second path with no shared component: a second Direct Connect location (the AWS Direct Connect Resiliency Toolkit guides this) and, for the most critical paths, a Site-to-Site VPN backup over the internet sized for critical traffic, because two Direct Connect locations still share the Direct Connect path into the Region. Run BGP on both paths, and alarm on connection and tunnel state (for example the Direct Connect ConnectionState and VPN TunnelState metrics).

content.displayText: Resilience in AWS Site-to-Site VPN
Direct Connect in AWS GovCloud (US)

Related AWS Post-Event Summary (Sep 2021): during an AWS Direct Connect event in the Tokyo Region, AWS VPN connectivity, which some customers use as a backup to Direct Connect, was not impacted, so give each private link a backup path that does not share its failure modes.
Monitor AWS Direct Connect with Amazon CloudWatch (ConnectionState)
Monitor AWS Site-to-Site VPN tunnels with Amazon CloudWatch (TunnelState)
Tunnel options for your AWS Site-to-Site VPN connection

choices.title: Failover between paths was tested in the last 12 months, and the backup path can carry critical traffic

helpfulResource.displayText: Good looks like: In the last 12 months a scheduled test took the primary path out of service, routing converged to the backup path within your recovery objective, and critical traffic ran over the backup path at expected peak volume within latency and error goals. Time to converge, results and fixes are recorded. Platform notes: Direct Connect: the Resiliency Toolkit failover test brings down a BGP peering session for a set time so you can verify that traffic moves to a redundant virtual interface. Site-to-Site VPN: take one tunnel down from the customer side and confirm traffic continues on the other. Partition notes: As of 2026-10-06, AWS Capabilities by Region lists the AWS Direct Connect Resiliency Toolkit in AWS GovCloud (US), but not its failover test (StartBgpFailoverTest). In GovCloud, test failover by shutting down the BGP session or connection from your customer router in a scheduled window, and confirm traffic moves to the redundant path; verify per Region.

improvementPlan.displayText: Schedule a failover test at least yearly and after network changes: announce it, take down the primary BGP session or connection in a low-risk window, measure time to converge and critical-path latency and errors over the backup path, restore the primary, and track fixes to closure. Add the scenario to your game day plan.

choices.title: On-premises dependencies on the critical path (identity, DNS, databases, mainframe) have their own tested recovery plan

helpfulResource.displayText: Good looks like: Each on-premises or partner system the critical path needs, such as identity providers and directories, DNS, databases, mainframes and file transfer, has a named owner, recovery objectives at least as strict as the workload's, and a recovery plan tested in the last 12 months. Where it fits, the workload removes the dependency from the critical path (for example by caching, by replicating data to AWS, or by running a directory replica or resolver in AWS) or degrades gracefully while it is unreachable. Platform notes: Hybrid DNS: Amazon Route 53 Resolver endpoints with IP addresses in more than one Availability Zone, forwarding to on-premises resolvers at more than one site. Partition notes: Route 53 Resolver endpoints are available in AWS GovCloud (US) as of 2026-10-06; verify per Region.

improvementPlan.displayText: List every on-premises and partner dependency on the critical path, agree recovery objectives with each owner, and get evidence of a recent recovery test. Where an owner cannot meet the workload's objectives, remove the hard dependency or add a degraded mode, and record the residual risk.

questions.title: Overload protection and tenant fairness
questions.description: Maximum risk: High (launch-blocking unless remediated or formally accepted). Category: Defense against overload. How do you stop one client, tenant or traffic source from overloading the workload and degrading it for everyone else? Out of scope if: the workload accepts no requests or events from users or other systems (rare). Mark the question as not applicable with that reason, and keep an inventory of entry points showing none. Evidence to collect: limit configuration per API, tenant or source. The last limit change and how long it took. Throttling and load-shedding metrics. The most recent surge test report.

helpfulResource.displayText: REL05-BP02 Throttle requests (AWS Well-Architected)

choices.title: Per-client, tenant, API key or source limits are enforced (or there is one trusted, bounded caller)

helpfulResource.displayText: Good looks like: Every entry point enforces a limit per caller identity (API key, tenant, account, or source IP for anonymous traffic), sized from measured capacity so no caller exceeds its share, and throttled callers get a fast, retryable response such as HTTP 429. Platform notes: EC2 and containers: AWS WAF rate-based rules at the edge, plus limits in the service or a sidecar. Amazon API Gateway: stage and method throttling, and usage plans with API keys (best-effort) for per-client fairness. AWS WAF rate-based rules on REST API stages, or on CloudFront in front of HTTP APIs, cannot be bypassed by callers but are approximate and can take minutes to engage, so keep precise per-tenant quotas in the service. Serverless: Lambda reserved concurrency. Partition notes: CloudFront is not available in AWS GovCloud (US) as of 2026-10-05; use AWS WAF on REST API stages or Application Load Balancers. Reader note: REL05-BP02 lists the discontinued Virtual Waiting Room on AWS solution; this practice does not need it.

improvementPlan.displayText: Inventory every entry point and caller type. Set per-caller quotas and rate limits from load test results, enforce them as close to the edge as possible, return a retryable throttling error, and alarm when a caller is throttled persistently. Document how a caller requests a higher limit.

content.displayText: Amazon API Gateway usage plans (best-effort limits for per-client fairness)

choices.title: Excess load is rejected or shed before expensive work, and queues are bounded so stale work is dropped or dead-lettered

helpfulResource.displayText: Good looks like: When demand exceeds capacity, the workload rejects excess work cheaply, before expensive steps such as heavy authentication or database work where possible, keeps serving admitted requests within latency goals, and never builds unbounded backlogs. Every queue has a maximum depth or age, and work older than its useful life is dropped or sent to a dead-letter queue. Platform notes: EC2 and containers: concurrency limits in the server and connection limits at the load balancer. Serverless: reserved concurrency, and Amazon SQS dead-letter queues with a maximum receive count. Asynchronous paths: alarm on the age of the oldest message.

improvementPlan.displayText: Measure the concurrency at which latency degrades and set admission limits below it. Prioritize health checks and critical calls, return fast errors for rejected work, bound every queue by size or age with a dead-letter destination, and confirm the behavior with a load test that exceeds capacity.

content.displayText: Related AWS Post-Event Summary (Dec 2021): clients that did not back off adequately drove congestion that also impaired monitoring, so shed excess work early and bound queues and retries.

choices.title: Limits can be changed, or a single source blocked, within minutes and without a code deployment

helpfulResource.displayText: Good looks like: An operator can raise or lower a limit, or block one abusive caller, within minutes through validated, versioned configuration that is rolled out safely, without building or deploying code. The steps are in the runbook and work during an incident. Platform notes: Typical levers: block a caller with AWS WAF IP sets or rate-based rules; change limits through dynamic configuration such as AWS AppConfig; tune per-client fairness with API Gateway usage plans (best-effort, not hard limits).

improvementPlan.displayText: Move limits into dynamic configuration with validation and a safe deployment strategy that rolls back on alarms, add runbook steps to change a limit and to block a caller, rehearse both in a game day, and record how long they take.

choices.title: A sudden surge from one client or tenant was tested, and the limits protected everyone else

helpfulResource.displayText: Good looks like: A load test drove one client or tenant far above its limit while representative traffic continued for everyone else, and showed that only the noisy caller was throttled, other callers stayed within latency and error goals, and the expected alarms fired. The AWS ORR whitepaper's example questions include planning for a surge from a single customer.

improvementPlan.displayText: Add a single-tenant surge scenario to the load test plan: ramp one caller to several times its limit, record per-caller latency and errors, verify throttling metrics and alarms, and fix any shared bottleneck the test exposes, such as connection pools, databases or downstream quotas. Run high-volume tests within the Amazon EC2 Testing Policy.

Alarms on rate-based rule and Anti-DDoS rule group metrics and where they page. The DDoS runbook and the date of its last rehearsal. For Shield Advanced subscribers, which web ACLs run the Anti-DDoS managed rule group after the auto-upgrade that starts 2026-10-25 (AWS Security Blog, as updated 2026-10-05) and whether IaC matches.

choices.title: The workload has no internet-facing endpoints

helpfulResource.displayText: Good looks like: Nothing in the workload accepts connections from the internet: no internet-facing load balancers, public API Gateway endpoints, Amazon CloudFront distributions, Lambda function URLs, public IP addresses or other public listeners, and users reach it only over private networks. improvementPlan.displayText: If any endpoint is reachable from the internet, including through a third-party CDN or front door, clear this statement and answer the other statements. Recheck when new entry points are added.

choices.title: Internet-facing endpoints use a web application firewall with managed and rate-based rules (network controls for non-HTTP)

helpfulResource.displayText: Good looks like: Every internet-facing HTTP endpoint has a web ACL with AWS managed rule groups for the application and at least one rate-based rule sized from measured traffic. New rules are tuned in Count mode, then set to Block, and web ACLs are managed as code. Non-HTTP endpoints use security groups, network ACLs or AWS Network Firewall, plus AWS Shield Standard. Platform notes: AWS WAF protects CloudFront, Application Load Balancers, API Gateway REST APIs, AppSync GraphQL APIs, Cognito user pools, Bedrock AgentCore Gateway, Verified Access and Amplify (as of 2026-10-06); front HTTP APIs with CloudFront and AWS WAF. Partition notes: As of 2026-10-06, AWS GovCloud (US) has AWS WAF with AWS managed, custom and rate-based rules, but no third-party seller rule groups, CloudFront or Shield Advanced; attach web ACLs to Application Load Balancers or REST API stages. Keep export-controlled data out of all AWS WAF metadata (names, conditions, string filters, regex pattern sets).

improvementPlan.displayText: List every internet-facing endpoint and associate a web ACL with each HTTP endpoint. Add AWS managed rule groups and a rate-based rule per entry point, aggregating by IP, forwarded IP or a custom key such as an API key header. Run new rules in Count mode against real traffic, then switch them to Block, and keep web ACLs in infrastructure as code. For non-HTTP endpoints, restrict sources with security groups and network ACLs, and consider AWS Network Firewall.

improvementPlan.displayText: Write the runbook from the AWS DDoS response guidance: detection signals, decision points, the rule changes to make and who approves them, support case severity and contacts, and communications. Rehearse it as a tabletop at least yearly and after major edge changes, and track gaps. If you subscribe to Shield Advanced, keep SRT access and proactive engagement contacts current.

questions.title: Health checks and safe capacity lifecycle
questions.description: Maximum risk: High (launch-blocking unless remediated or formally accepted). Category: Blast radius containment. Do health checks remove or replace unhealthy capacity automatically, without letting a shared dependency failure or the checks themselves take healthy capacity out of service, and do new capacity and versions enter and leave service safely? Out of scope if: all compute is platform-managed (for example AWS Lambda). Select the first statement and keep the evidence. Evidence to collect: health check configuration per tier (what it tests, interval, thresholds and the action on failure). How the checks behave when a shared dependency fails. Readiness, warm-up and draining settings. A recent deployment or scale-in that shows no failed requests.

helpfulResource.displayText: REL11-BP03 Automate healing on all layers (AWS Well-Architected)

choices.title: All compute is platform-managed (for example AWS Lambda), with no self-managed instances, tasks or pods

helpfulResource.displayText: Good looks like: Every compute component is a service whose health AWS manages, for example AWS Lambda, which runs functions in multiple Availability Zones. There are no EC2 instances, Amazon ECS tasks (including tasks on AWS Fargate), Kubernetes pods or other servers that you place behind a load balancer or scale yourself. Evidence to collect: a compute inventory from your infrastructure as code or AWS Config that shows only platform-managed compute. When this is selected, the other statements do not change the score.

improvementPlan.displayText: If any instance, task or pod is on the critical path, clear this statement and answer the other statements. Platform-managed compute still needs alarms and safe deployments, which other questions score.

choices.title: Health checks test the ability to serve, and failed instances, tasks or pods are replaced or removed automatically

helpfulResource.displayText: Good looks like: Each tier has a health check that exercises the ability to serve requests, not only that the process is running, and a failed check removes the unit from traffic and replaces it automatically, with no operator action. Thresholds avoid flapping, and an alarm fires when unhealthy counts or replacements rise above normal. Platform notes: EC2: Auto Scaling groups with Elastic Load Balancing health checks turned on, so instances that fail load balancer checks are replaced. Containers: Amazon ECS container health checks and load balancer checks, or Kubernetes liveness and readiness probes, with an ECS service or Kubernetes Deployment that restores the desired count.

improvementPlan.displayText: For each tier, define a health check that covers the ability to serve, connect it to automatic removal and replacement (Auto Scaling group ELB health checks, an ECS service or a Kubernetes controller), tune intervals and thresholds from observed behavior, and alarm on unhealthy host counts and replacement rate. Test it by failing one unit and confirming it is replaced without customer impact.

choices.title: Checks separate local from shared-dependency failure, so a dependency outage cannot remove all healthy capacity

helpfulResource.displayText: Good looks like: Health checks that drive replacement test only local health, and dependency failures are reported through separate metrics and alarms. Where deep checks that include dependencies drive routing, the system fails open when every unit fails at once instead of removing all capacity. Platform notes: EC2: an Application Load Balancer routes to all targets when every target in a target group is unhealthy (fail open), but an Auto Scaling group that uses ELB health checks can still replace those instances, so keep dependency calls out of checks that trigger replacement. Containers: keep dependency calls out of ECS container health checks and Kubernetes liveness probes.

improvementPlan.displayText: Review each health check: remove calls to shared dependencies from checks that trigger replacement or removal, report dependency health as separate metrics and alarms, confirm fail-open behavior in each load balancer and service mesh, and verify in a test environment that blocking a shared dependency leaves capacity in service.

choices.title: New capacity and versions pass readiness checks before taking traffic, and drain in-flight work before stopping

helpfulResource.displayText: Good looks like: New instances, tasks, pods and versions get traffic only after a readiness check confirms they started correctly and warmed up. Units leaving service during deployments, scale-in or replacement stop taking new work and finish or hand off in-flight requests and jobs before they stop. The AWS ORR whitepaper's example questions ask for on-host validation before a deployment re-registers with the load balancer. Platform notes: EC2: Auto Scaling lifecycle hooks, Application Load Balancer slow start and deregistration delay, and AWS CodeDeploy ValidateService hooks. Containers: ECS health check grace period and container stop timeout with termination-signal handling; Kubernetes readiness probes and preStop hooks.

improvementPlan.displayText: Add a readiness or validation step to every deployment and launch path, use warm-up or slow start where cold units are slow, make processes stop intake and finish in-flight work on a termination signal, set draining and stop timeouts longer than your longest normal request, and confirm with a deployment under load that no requests fail.

questions.title: Peak demand, quotas and capacity headroom
questions.description: Maximum risk: High (launch-blocking unless remediated or formally accepted). Category: Defense against overload. Do quotas, scaling limits and capacity cover forecast peak demand plus failover in every account and Region the workload uses, with enough lead time to get more? Evidence to collect: the demand forecast (normal and peak, key event dates, growth and failover scenarios) and who approved it. Current quotas and scaling ceilings compared with forecast peak plus failover in each account and Region. Quota usage alarms. Capacity reservations or scheduled scaling, and measured scaling lead times.

helpfulResource.displayText: REL01-BP01 Aware of service quotas (AWS Well-Architected)

choices.title: Normal and peak demand, key event dates and failover scenarios are forecast and documented

helpfulResource.displayText: Good looks like: A documented forecast, owned jointly by the business owner and the engineering team, gives normal and peak demand in the units each component scales on (requests, messages, sessions, data volume), daily and seasonal patterns, known event dates such as deadlines, launches or enrollment periods, expected growth over the next 12 months, and the extra load each component takes when an Availability Zone or Region fails over. It is reviewed at least quarterly and before each known event. REL01-BP01 lists not assessing capacity needs before a new customer event as an anti-pattern.

improvementPlan.displayText: Build the forecast from historical metrics and business plans: choose the scaling unit for each component, record peaks and their timing, add known event dates and growth, and calculate each component's load when one Availability Zone or the primary Region fails. Get the business owner's sign-off, review it quarterly, and use it as the input for quotas, capacity and the load test.

choices.title: Quotas and scaling ceilings in every account and Region, including recovery Regions, cover peak plus failover and are alarmed

helpfulResource.displayText: Good looks like: Every quota and limit the workload can reach (service quotas, account concurrency and throughput limits, Auto Scaling maximums, IP space, third-party API limits) covers forecast peak plus failover with a documented margin in every production account and Region, including recovery Regions, and CloudWatch alarms fire on usage well before each limit. Fixed quotas are designed around. Platform notes: Serverless: Lambda account concurrency and per-function scaling rate. EC2 and containers: vCPU-based instance quotas, Auto Scaling and capacity provider maximums, and subnet IP space. Partition notes: Service Quotas is available in AWS GovCloud (US) as of 2026-10-05, but quota request templates are not (checked 2026-10-06), so request GovCloud increases per account. Reader note: REL01-BP01, BP02 and BP06 list Amazon DevOps Guru (no new customers from 2026-10-29), and REL01-BP01 and BP02 list Amazon CodeGuru Reviewer (no new repository associations since 2025-11-07); neither is needed here.

improvementPlan.displayText: Inventory the quotas and limits each component can reach, compare them with forecast peak plus failover in every production and recovery account and Region, request increases with enough lead time, alarm on usage at a threshold you choose (for example 80 percent), and recheck after each forecast update. Where supported, use quota request templates so new accounts start with the quotas you need.

helpfulResource.displayText: Good looks like: For each component you know how long adding capacity takes (instance launch and warm-up, task and pod start, cache warm-up, throughput changes), and capacity for the documented peak is already running, scheduled ahead of known peaks, or reserved where launches might be constrained. Set Auto Scaling minimums so scale-in cannot remove required headroom, and alarm when running capacity falls below target.

questions.description: Maximum risk: High (launch-blocking unless remediated or formally accepted). Category: Defense against overload. Has the workload been load tested at or above forecast peak with margin, do you know where and how it breaks, and did alarms and scaling work during the test? Penetration testing is scored in the security launch gate question. High-volume tests follow the Amazon EC2 Testing Policy. The alarms, scaling events and runbook steps observed during the test.

helpfulResource.displayText: REL07-BP04 Load test your workload (AWS Well-Architected)

choices.title: A production-like environment was load tested at or above forecast peak with representative traffic since the last major change

helpfulResource.displayText: Good looks like: Since the last major architecture or capacity change, a production-like environment (same IaC, instance or task sizes, data volume, caches, quotas and dependency settings as production, or production itself in a scheduled window) sustained at least forecast peak plus your documented margin, within latency and error goals. The report is kept with the review. Platform notes: EC2 and containers: include scale-out from minimum capacity and the time to add capacity, not only steady state. Serverless: test with the account and function concurrency, API and downstream quotas you will run with, including bursts. Asynchronous paths: include queue and stream throughput and consumer lag.

improvementPlan.displayText: Write down forecast peak and the margin you need (for example twice peak, or peak with one Availability Zone lost). Build a traffic model from production logs or business forecasts, generate load from enough distributed sources (for example the Distributed Load Testing on AWS solution or an open-source tool), stub or coordinate third-party calls, and test in a production-like environment. Compare results with latency and error goals, fix what fails, and repeat after every major change. Follow the Amazon EC2 Testing Policy for high-volume tests.

questions.title: Recovery objectives and proven recovery
questions.description: Maximum risk: High (launch-blocking unless remediated or formally accepted). Category: Data recovery. Have the business and the team agreed recovery time and recovery point objectives (RTO and RPO) for each component, and have restores and failovers proven that you can meet them? Evidence to collect: RTO and RPO per component with the business owner's approval. The DR strategy, including the Region decision and residency constraints. The date, scope and measured RTO and RPO of the last end-to-end restore test and of the last failover and failback exercise.

helpfulResource.displayText: REL13-BP03 Test DR implementation (AWS Well-Architected)

choices.title: RTO and RPO are defined per component from business impact and approved by the business owner

helpfulResource.displayText: Good looks like: Each component and data store has a recovery time objective (how long it may be unavailable) and a recovery point objective (how much data may be lost), derived from the business impact of downtime and data loss on the critical journeys it supports. The business owner approved them, they are recorded where the team and incident responders can find them, and each dependency's objectives are at least as strict as those of the components that need it. Objectives are reviewed when the workload or its criticality changes.

improvementPlan.displayText: Run a business impact analysis with the business owner: for each critical journey, estimate the cost of downtime and of data loss over time, set RTO and RPO per component, check that dependencies (including third parties and shared platforms) can meet them, and record the approved values. Revisit them at each major change and at least yearly.

content.displayText: AWS Resilience Hub resiliency policies (record and assess RTO and RPO targets)

choices.title: An end-to-end restore was tested in the last 12 months and met RTO and RPO (or there is no persistent state)

helpfulResource.displayText: Good looks like: In the last 12 months the team restored the workload's persistent data from backups into a working environment, brought the application up on it, validated the data and a critical journey end to end, and measured elapsed time and the data-loss window against RTO and RPO. Results, gaps and fixes are recorded. The practice may be in-house or provided by your operations partner under contract, with evidence you can inspect. If there is no persistent state, the evidence is a data inventory showing that every store can be rebuilt from source. Partition notes: AWS Backup restore testing is not available in AWS GovCloud (US) as of 2026-10-05; there, script on-demand restore jobs and validation checks instead; verify per Region.

improvementPlan.displayText: Schedule a restore test at least yearly and after major changes: take the latest recovery point of every critical data store, restore it into an isolated account or environment, start the application against it, run data validation and a critical-journey test, and record the elapsed time and the age of the restored data against RTO and RPO. Automate the test where possible and track every gap to closure.

content.displayText: REL09-BP04 Perform periodic recovery of the data to verify backup integrity and processes

choices.title: A documented DR strategy meets RTO and RPO, including a deliberate single- or multi-Region decision and residency constraints

helpfulResource.displayText: Good looks like: A documented DR strategy (backup and restore, pilot light, warm standby, or multi-site active/active) is chosen per component to meet its RTO and RPO. It records a deliberate decision to recover within one Region or into another Region, the scenarios it covers and excludes (component failure, Availability Zone loss, Regional impairment, data corruption), the residency constraints on where copies may live, and the cost accepted. Where RTO is short, recovery relies on data-plane operations and capacity that already exists. Partition notes: In AWS GovCloud (US), the recovery Region for a GovCloud workload is the other GovCloud Region; Amazon S3 objects and Amazon RDS and Amazon EBS snapshots cannot be copied directly between GovCloud and other AWS Regions, as of 2026-10-05. ARC Region switch is available in both GovCloud Regions; verify per Region.

improvementPlan.displayText: For each component, compare the DR strategies with its RTO, RPO and budget, choose one, and document the Region decision, the scenarios covered and excluded, residency constraints, the recovery runbook and the dependencies the recovery itself needs. Prefer recovery steps that use data-plane operations and pre-provisioned capacity. Review the strategy when objectives or architecture change.

choices.title: Failover to the recovery environment and failback were exercised in the last 12 months, with achieved RTO and RPO recorded

helpfulResource.displayText: Good looks like: In the last 12 months the team failed the workload over to its recovery environment (another account or Region, as the DR strategy says) with the documented runbook and the same tools it would use in a real event, served traffic or a representative test load there, and then failed back. Achieved RTO and RPO, steps that failed, and configuration drift found between the primary and recovery environments are recorded and fixed.

improvementPlan.displayText: Plan a failover exercise at least yearly: set success criteria from RTO and RPO, run the failover with the documented runbook and tools in a scheduled window (or in a production-like copy until production failover is proven safe), measure time to recover and data loss, fail back, and track fixes. Detect configuration drift between the environments continuously so that the recovery environment matches production.

questions.title: Recovery from corruption, deletion and ransomware
questions.description: Maximum risk: High (launch-blocking unless remediated or formally accepted). Category: Data recovery. Can you recover critical data to a known-good point after corruption, accidental or malicious deletion, or ransomware, even if production credentials are compromised? Out of scope if: the workload stores no persistent data and every store can be rebuilt from source (mark the question as not applicable with that reason and keep the data inventory as evidence). Evidence to collect: the inventory of critical data stores with their point-in-time recovery, versioning or backup settings and retention. The backup account, vault lock and key policy configuration. Alarms for anomalous deletes, writes or encryption. The date and result of the last rehearsed restore to a point before a simulated corruption.

helpfulResource.displayText: REL09-BP02 Secure and encrypt backups (AWS Well-Architected)

choices.title: Point-in-time recovery, versioning or frequent backups protect every critical data store

helpfulResource.displayText: Good looks like: Every critical data store is covered: databases have point-in-time recovery or continuous backups, object stores have versioning, and other stores have frequent automated backups, with a recovery point interval that meets RPO and retention long enough to reach back before corruption is likely to be noticed (often weeks, not days). Replicas, standbys and multi-Region tables do not count as backups, because they copy corruption and deletes too. A workload with no persistent data marks the whole question as not applicable instead. Platform notes: Examples: point-in-time recovery for Amazon DynamoDB, Amazon RDS and Amazon Aurora; S3 Versioning; scheduled Amazon EBS snapshots; AWS Backup continuous backups. EC2 and containers: include data on volumes and file systems, not only databases. Serverless: include queues, streams or caches that hold the only copy of data.

improvementPlan.displayText: Inventory every data store and classify it by criticality. Turn on point-in-time recovery or versioning where supported, add automated backups elsewhere through a central backup plan, set retention from how long corruption could go unnoticed, and alarm on failed backup jobs and on stores that are not covered. Document which data can be rebuilt from source instead.

content.displayText: Point-in-time backups for Amazon DynamoDB
Retaining multiple versions of objects with S3 Versioning

choices.title: Backups are immutable and isolated from production credentials, ideally in a separate account (for example Vault Lock)

helpfulResource.displayText: Good looks like: Copies of critical backups are kept where production identities, pipelines and administrators cannot delete them or shorten their retention: immutable retention (for example AWS Backup Vault Lock or Amazon S3 Object Lock, each in compliance mode), ideally in a separate backup account with its own access controls and always outside the reach of production credentials, with encryption keys that a compromised production account cannot disable or delete. The Well-Architected Framework lists using the same security domain for production and backup systems, and not implementing immutability, as anti-patterns. Platform notes: AWS Backup logically air-gapped vaults combine locked retention with sharing for recovery into another account. Partition notes: AWS Backup logically air-gapped vaults are not available in AWS GovCloud (US) as of 2026-10-05; use compliance-mode Vault Lock on a vault in a separate backup account with cross-account copy, or S3 Object Lock in compliance mode; verify per Region.

improvementPlan.displayText: Create a dedicated backup account, copy critical recovery points to a locked vault there (compliance-mode Vault Lock or a logically air-gapped vault), restrict who can change backup and key policies with permission guardrails such as service control policies, keep backup keys out of reach of production administrators, and alarm on attempts to delete recovery points or change vault, lock or key settings. Test that you can restore from the isolated copy into a clean account.

content.displayText: Creating backup copies across AWS accounts (AWS Backup)
Locking objects with Amazon S3 Object Lock

choices.title: Integrity checks or alarms detect anomalous deletes, writes or encryption of critical data

helpfulResource.displayText: Good looks like: The team learns about corruption, mass deletion or ransomware-style encryption in time to restore from a point before it began: alarms watch unusual delete or overwrite rates, write volume, record or object counts and permission or encryption changes; scheduled integrity checks (checksums, invariants, reconciliation with a source of record) run on critical data; threat detection flags anomalous data access; and recovery points are scanned for malware before use. Alarms page the data owner, and the runbook says how to find the last known-good point. Platform notes: Examples: Amazon GuardDuty S3 Protection findings for anomalous deletes; GuardDuty Malware Protection for AWS Backup to scan recovery points; CloudWatch alarms on integrity metrics; Amazon S3 checksums. Partition notes: In AWS GovCloud (US), GuardDuty Malware Protection for AWS Backup does not scan Amazon EC2 or Amazon EBS recovery points as of 2026-10-06; scan restored copies in an isolated account instead; verify per Region.

improvementPlan.displayText: For each critical store, define what abnormal looks like (delete and overwrite rates, record counts, write volume, encryption or permission changes) and alarm on it; add scheduled integrity checks that compare data with its source of record; turn on threat detection for data stores; scan recovery points for malware; and document in the runbook how to identify the last known-good recovery point.

content.displayText: Checking object integrity in Amazon S3

choices.title: Restoring to a point before a simulated corruption was rehearsed, and the restored data was validated

helpfulResource.displayText: Good looks like: The team rehearsed a corruption scenario in a non-production copy, for example a bad batch job, a faulty migration or mass-deleted records: it identified the last known-good point, restored to it from the isolated backup copy, validated the restored data with integrity checks and a critical journey, and reconciled or replayed changes made after that point. Time to detect, decide and restore was recorded against RTO and RPO, and the runbook was updated. Partition notes: AWS Backup restore testing is not available in AWS GovCloud (US) as of 2026-10-05; script the restore and validation steps instead; verify per Region.

improvementPlan.displayText: Add a corruption drill to the recovery test plan: in a non-production copy, inject a realistic corruption or deletion, practice finding the last known-good point, restore from the isolated backup copy into a clean environment, run validation, and reconcile later changes. Record the timings, fix gaps in tooling and runbooks, and repeat at least yearly.

questions.title: Restart and scale out while dependencies are impaired
questions.description: Maximum risk: Medium (not launch-blocking, remediate on a plan). Category: Service restart. Can the workload start from zero, restart, or scale out quickly while dependencies such as artifact repositories, configuration stores or the internet are impaired? Out of scope if: every component is a managed service with no start-up path you control (mark the question as not applicable with that reason). Evidence to collect: the restart-from-zero runbook with expected timings. The source of every image, package and binary used at start-up. Configuration and secret caching behavior. The date and duration of the last cold-start exercise.

helpfulResource.displayText: REL11-BP05 Use static stability (AWS Well-Architected)

choices.title: A restart-from-zero procedure documents start-up order and has no circular dependencies

helpfulResource.displayText: Good looks like: A tested runbook brings the whole workload up from nothing, lists the start-up order of components and dependencies with expected timings against RTO, and confirms there are no circular dependencies, for example a service that needs a configuration store that itself needs the service. The AWS ORR whitepaper's example questions ask for restart RTO, a runbook and circular-dependency analysis.

improvementPlan.displayText: Draw the start-up dependency graph, break any cycles (for example by caching or bundling bootstrap data), write the runbook with expected timings, and review it after each major architecture change.

content.displayText: Related AWS Post-Event Summary (Feb 2017): systems that had not been completely restarted for many years took longer than expected to restart, so exercise full restarts before you need them.

choices.title: Images, packages and binaries needed to deploy, restart or scale come from repositories you control, not the internet

helpfulResource.displayText: Good looks like: Every artifact needed to launch capacity (container images, machine images, OS and language packages, agents and models) is stored in repositories you operate, in every Region you run in, so an outage, rate limit or deleted package in a public registry cannot stop a restart or scale-out. Platform notes: Containers: Amazon ECR with pull through cache rules for upstream registries. EC2: pre-built machine images and a package mirror you operate. Serverless: deployment packages and layers in your own accounts. Packages: AWS CodeArtifact upstream repositories. Partition notes: AWS CodeArtifact is not available in AWS GovCloud (US) as of 2026-10-05; there, use Amazon ECR private repositories (ECR-to-ECR pull through cache rules work only within the partition), Amazon S3-hosted mirrors or a self-managed repository inside the partition; verify per Region.

improvementPlan.displayText: List every external artifact source used at start-up and scale-out (check user data, Dockerfiles, bootstrap scripts and agents), mirror each into a repository you control and replicate it to every Region you use, block direct internet fetches at start-up, and alarm on failed pulls.

content.displayText: AWS CodeArtifact upstream repositories (where available)

choices.title: Start-up survives an outage of the configuration, secrets or feature-flag store by using replicated or last-known-good values

helpfulResource.displayText: Good looks like: If the configuration, secrets or feature-flag store is slow or unavailable, new and restarting instances still start with last-known-good values (for example a local cache, the AWS AppConfig Agent cache, or values bundled at build time), secrets needed for recovery are replicated to the recovery Region, and start-up never waits on a control-plane call that could be impaired by the same event.

improvementPlan.displayText: List every configuration, secret and flag read at start-up, cache last-known-good values with integrity checks, replicate recovery secrets across Regions, give start-up calls timeouts with safe defaults, and test start-up with the configuration store blocked.

choices.title: A cold start or large scale-out was exercised in the last 12 months with external dependencies blocked, within RTO

helpfulResource.displayText: Good looks like: In the last 12 months, in a production-like environment, you restarted the workload from zero, or scaled out several times over, while internet access was blocked and non-critical dependencies were impaired, and recovery completed within RTO. Results and fixes are recorded.

improvementPlan.displayText: Schedule a cold-start exercise at least yearly: block egress to the internet and to non-critical dependencies in a test environment (for example with AWS FIS network actions or security group changes), restart or scale out, measure time to healthy, and track fixes to closure.

questions.title: Changes only through reviewed pipelines and IaC, including emergencies
questions.description: Maximum risk: High (launch-blocking unless remediated or formally accepted). Category: Deployment safety. Is every production change, including infrastructure, configuration, feature flags and changes proposed by scripts, bots or AI agents, reviewed by someone other than its author and applied only through pipelines, even during emergencies? Evidence to collect: the list of production change paths (IaC, application configuration, feature flags, pipelines, database changes). Repository protection rules and pipeline permissions. Which people and roles can change production outside the pipeline, and the guardrails that stop them. Drift detection results and alarms. The emergency change procedure and the audit record of its last use.

helpfulResource.displayText: REL08-BP05 Deploy changes with automation (AWS Well-Architected)

choices.title: Infrastructure, configuration, feature-flag and pipeline changes are version-controlled and deployed only by pipelines

helpfulResource.displayText: Good looks like: Application code, IaC, application and feature-flag configuration, database schema changes and the pipeline definitions themselves live in version control, and every planned production change is applied by the pipeline from a reviewed commit. A change made outside the pipeline raises an alarm. Human write access (read-only defaults or time-bound elevation) is scored in event_mutating_access. The practice may be in-house or provided by your operations partner under contract, with evidence you can inspect. Platform notes: EC2: build images in a pipeline and replace instances instead of changing them by hand. Containers: deploy image digests through the pipeline. Serverless: deploy functions, layers and APIs with IaC. Flags: a configuration service with a deployment strategy. Partition notes: In AWS GovCloud (US), CodePipeline cross-Region actions are not available and third-party source connections work only in AWS GovCloud (US-East), as of 2026-10-05; verify per Region.

improvementPlan.displayText: Inventory every way production changes today (console, CLI, scripts, configuration tools, feature-flag dashboards, database clients). Move each into version control with a pipeline deployment, restrict human write access as event_mutating_access describes, and alarm when a change is made outside the pipeline.

choices.title: Every change, including from scripts, bots or AI agents, is reviewed by someone other than its author, enforced technically

helpfulResource.displayText: Good looks like: Repository protection rules or an equivalent control require approval by at least one person other than the author before any change that reaches production can merge or deploy: application code, IaC, configuration, feature flags, canaries, operations tools and pipeline definitions. Changes proposed by scripts, bots or AI agents are reviewed by an accountable human, and no bot or agent can approve its own change or bypass review. Administrators cannot skip the rule without an audited exception. For automation that acts on its own at run time (scaling, automated remediation, scheduled jobs), the automation's code and configuration are reviewed; individual runs within those reviewed bounds are not separate changes. The AWS ORR whitepaper's example questions score the absence of this review as High risk.

improvementPlan.displayText: Turn on protection rules for every repository that feeds production (required review by someone other than the author, no direct pushes, no self-approval, required status checks), apply them to bot and AI agent identities too, restrict who can change the rules or the pipeline's checks, and make the pipeline deploy only reviewed commits from protected branches. Audit regularly for bypasses.

choices.title: IaC changes are previewed before apply, and drift is detected and alarmed

helpfulResource.displayText: Good looks like: Every IaC change shows a reviewed preview of what will be created, changed, replaced or deleted before it is applied (for example CloudFormation change sets or a Terraform plan), and replacing or deleting a stateful resource needs explicit approval. The deletion and replacement guards themselves (for example a Retain deletion policy, stack policies and termination protection) are scored in event_operator_tooling_safety. Drift between deployed resources and their templates is checked on a schedule and alarms the owner, and drift is fixed through the pipeline.

improvementPlan.displayText: Make the pipeline produce and publish an IaC preview for review, fail or require approval when a change replaces or deletes a stateful resource, and schedule drift detection (for example the AWS Config managed rule cloudformation-stack-drift-detection-check) with an alarm to the owner. Fix drift by changing code, not by hand.

content.displayText: AWS Config managed rule cloudformation-stack-drift-detection-check

choices.title: A documented emergency path still uses the pipeline and review, may override windows and bake time, and is audited

helpfulResource.displayText: Good looks like: For urgent fixes, a documented emergency path ships through the same pipeline: a reviewer is still required (any available engineer, at any hour), and only time-based controls such as deployment windows, bake time or the number of waves may be shortened, by a named approver. Direct production access is kept for cases the pipeline cannot handle, through an audited break-glass role that alarms on use. Every emergency change is recorded, reviewed afterwards and reconciled with code, and the path was used or rehearsed in the last 12 months.

improvementPlan.displayText: Write the emergency change procedure: who can invoke it, which pipeline controls may be shortened and which never are (review, safety tests, rollback), and how break-glass access is granted, alarmed and revoked. Add a pipeline option that skips only time-based gates with a recorded approver, rehearse the path in a game day, and review every use within a few days.
