questions.title: Pre-production parity and automated test gates
questions.description: Maximum risk: High (launch-blocking unless remediated or formally accepted). Category: Deployment safety. Before a change reaches production, does it pass automated tests in representative pre-production environments, and does a failed test stop it from being promoted? Evidence to collect: the pipeline definition showing pre-production stages and their test actions. The last test failure that blocked promotion. How pre-production accounts, IaC and configuration differ from production. Build scan types and severity thresholds. Performance test results for the last release.

helpfulResource.displayText: REL08-BP02 Integrate functional testing (AWS Well-Architected)

choices.title: Automated integration and end-to-end tests run in pre-production after each deployment and block promotion on failure

helpfulResource.displayText: Good looks like: After every deployment to pre-production, the pipeline runs automated integration and end-to-end tests against the deployed stack, covering each critical journey and the APIs it calls, and promotion stops when any test fails. Overrides are audited. Infrastructure and configuration changes are tested like code. Platform notes: EC2: validation scripts in AWS CodeDeploy lifecycle hooks, or a test stage after deployment. Containers: tests against the new Amazon ECS service revision before traffic shifts, for example with ECS deployment lifecycle hooks. Serverless: tests against the new Lambda version, for example in a CodeDeploy BeforeAllowTraffic hook. Any pipeline: an AWS CodeBuild test action in AWS CodePipeline, or your CI/CD system's equivalent. Partition notes: Amazon ECS deployment lifecycle hooks, part of ECS built-in blue/green, linear and canary deployments, are available in AWS GovCloud (US) as of 2026-10-06.

improvementPlan.displayText: Add a pre-production stage to every pipeline (code, infrastructure and configuration) that deploys the change and then runs automated integration and end-to-end tests for each critical journey. Make any failed test fail the stage so promotion stops, notify the owning team, and treat flaky tests as defects to fix rather than tests to disable. Review the coverage of critical journeys at each ORR.

choices.title: Pre-production uses the same IaC, pipeline, configuration shape and immutable artifact as production, in separate accounts

helpfulResource.displayText: Good looks like: Pre-production is built from the same infrastructure as code, pipeline definition and configuration structure as production, differing only in documented parameters such as size, endpoints and secrets, and it runs in AWS accounts separate from production. Each artifact (container image, function package, machine image or bundle) is built once, stored immutably with a version or digest, and that exact artifact is promoted through every stage; nothing is rebuilt or patched in place for production. Platform notes: EC2: bake machine images in an image pipeline (for example EC2 Image Builder) and replace instances rather than patching them in place. Containers: deploy by image digest and turn on Amazon ECR tag immutability. Serverless: promote the same published Lambda version or deployment package through each stage.

improvementPlan.displayText: Template every environment from the same IaC with per-environment parameters, move pre-production into its own accounts, build each artifact once and promote it by digest or version, and add a pipeline check that fails if the artifact about to reach production differs from the one tested in pre-production. Record any intended difference between environments and why it is safe. Reader note: This page refers to AWS App Mesh, which reached end of support on 2026-09-30; for canary deployments on Amazon ECS, use ECS built-in canary deployments instead.

choices.title: Unit tests, static analysis, and dependency, secret and IaC scans fail the build above an agreed severity

helpfulResource.displayText: Good looks like: Every build runs unit tests, static analysis, dependency (software composition) analysis, secret detection and IaC checks, and fails on any finding at or above the severity agreed with the security owner, for example critical or high. Thresholds are written down; exceptions carry an expiry date. Platform notes: Any platform: IaC checks such as cfn-lint, AWS CloudFormation Guard or CloudFormation Hooks; vulnerability scanning of container images in Amazon ECR and of Lambda functions with Amazon Inspector; and your static analysis and secret scanning tools run in AWS CodeBuild or your CI system. Partition notes: Amazon Inspector Lambda code scanning and code repository scanning are not available in AWS GovCloud (US) as of 2026-10-06; use Inspector image and package scanning plus your own static analysis there. Reader note: This page refers to Amazon CodeGuru Security, which was discontinued on 2025-11-20; any static analysis and secret scanning tool meets this practice.

improvementPlan.displayText: Add the missing scan types to the build, run them in report-only mode first to baseline existing findings, agree severity thresholds with the security owner, then make findings at or above the threshold fail the build. Route findings to the owning team, record time-bound exceptions, and review the thresholds at each ORR.

choices.title: Latency and throughput regressions are caught in pre-production for performance-sensitive paths (or there are none)

helpfulResource.displayText: Good looks like: For each performance-sensitive path, a repeatable load or benchmark test runs in pre-production for every release candidate, compares latency percentiles, throughput, errors and resource use with the last good baseline, and blocks promotion when a regression exceeds the agreed threshold. If no path is performance-sensitive, that decision and its reason are recorded. Platform notes: EC2 and containers: include CPU, memory and connection-pool use in the comparison. Serverless: compare function duration, concurrency and cold-start latency at the same load.

improvementPlan.displayText: Pick the performance-sensitive paths, define a short, representative load profile, record a baseline from the last good release, run the test automatically in a pre-production stage, and fail promotion when p99 latency, error rate or throughput regress beyond the agreed threshold. Run high-volume tests within the Amazon EC2 Testing Policy.

questions.title: Phased production rollout with automated stage gates
questions.description: Maximum risk: High (launch-blocking unless remediated or formally accepted). Category: Deployment safety. Does every production change, including configuration and feature flags, reach a small slice of capacity or traffic first and then expand in automated stages that stop when something goes wrong? Evidence to collect: deployment settings for each change type (code, infrastructure, configuration, feature flags) showing the first slice and later stages. The bake time and alarms watched in each stage. The order of Regions or cells, if any. Deployment window and blocker settings. The last rollout that a stage gate stopped.

helpfulResource.displayText: OPS06-BP03 Safe deployment strategies (AWS Well-Architected)

choices.title: Each production change, including configuration and flags, first reaches a small slice, then expands in automated, gated stages

helpfulResource.displayText: Good looks like: No production change goes to all capacity or users at once. Code, configuration and flag changes first reach a small slice (one instance, task or cell, or a few percent of requests or targets), then expand in automated stages, each only when the previous stage's health checks and alarms are clear. Any stage can stop the rollout. Infrastructure changes that cannot be split are applied one account, Region or stack at a time where there is more than one. Platform notes: EC2: AWS CodeDeploy deployment configurations that update a small batch first, or EC2 Auto Scaling instance refresh with checkpoints. Containers: Amazon ECS canary or linear deployments, or a progressive delivery controller on Amazon EKS. Serverless: Lambda alias traffic shifting with CodeDeploy canary or linear configurations. Configuration and flags: AWS AppConfig deployment strategies. Infrastructure: one pipeline stage per account or Region.

improvementPlan.displayText: For each change type, choose a native phased mechanism and configure a small first slice followed by automated increments, each gated on health checks and alarms. Remove or restrict any path, such as console edits or direct configuration pushes, that can apply a change everywhere at once. All-at-once deployment is a launch-blocking gap unless the accountable owner formally accepts it, for example for commercial software that supports only in-place upgrades.

choices.title: Multi-Region or cell-based workloads roll out one Region or cell at a time, and single-Region workloads use percentage stages

helpfulResource.displayText: Good looks like: Multi-Region or cell-based workloads deploy to one Region or cell first and then to the rest in waves of increasing size, so a bad change is much more likely to be caught in one Region or cell before it reaches the rest. Single-Region workloads use percentage stages within the Region, and may also stage by Availability Zone where the tooling supports it. The order of Regions, cells or zones is fixed in the pipeline definition, not left to the operator. Platform notes: EC2: AWS CodeDeploy zonal configuration deploys to one Availability Zone at a time, with a monitor duration between zones. Any platform: one pipeline stage per Region or cell, in a fixed order, each waiting for the previous stage to finish baking. Partition notes: AWS CodePipeline cross-Region actions are not available in AWS GovCloud (US) as of 2026-10-06; there, run a pipeline in each GovCloud (US) Region and promote between them in a fixed order.

improvementPlan.displayText: Order Regions or cells from lowest to highest risk, start with a single Region or cell, then promote in waves of increasing size with bake time between waves. Encode the order in the pipeline rather than a runbook, and make each wave wait until the previous one has finished baking with clear alarms.

content.displayText: Fault-isolated, zonal deployments with AWS CodeDeploy (AWS DevOps Blog)

choices.title: Each stage bakes under monitoring for longer than its rollback alarms take to evaluate, longest in early stages

helpfulResource.displayText: Good looks like: After each stage completes, the rollout waits for a defined bake time while automated monitoring watches alarms and canaries, and it promotes only if they stay clear. Each stage's bake time exceeds the evaluation time of the rollback alarms it watches (the alarm period multiplied by its evaluation periods, plus any delay in the metric arriving), so an alarm can fire before the next stage starts. The first stages, where a change first meets real traffic, bake longest, long enough to surface slow-burning problems and to include representative traffic; later stages can bake for less, but never for less than that evaluation time. Platform notes: EC2: the CodeDeploy zonal monitor duration, with a longer first-zone duration. Containers: Amazon ECS bake time in blue/green, linear and canary deployments. Serverless: the interval in CodeDeploy canary or linear configurations for Lambda aliases. Configuration and flags: the AWS AppConfig bake time after a deployment reaches all targets.

improvementPlan.displayText: For every production stage, list the rollback alarms it watches and their evaluation time, then set a bake time longer than the slowest of them, longest in the first stages. Watch customer-facing alarms and canaries during each bake, and revisit bake times after any incident that a longer bake would have caught.

choices.title: Automated blockers stop deployments outside approved windows, on blocked or peak dates, and during active alarms

helpfulResource.displayText: Good looks like: The pipeline itself refuses to start a production stage outside approved deployment windows (for example when the on-call team is not staffed to respond), on dates the business has blocked, such as peak or event days, and while relevant alarms are firing. A documented, audited override exists for urgent fixes. Platform notes: AWS CodePipeline: stage entry conditions with the DeploymentWindow rule (a cron expression) and the CloudWatchAlarm rule. Other CI/CD systems: an equivalent check before each production stage against a change calendar and the current alarm state.

improvementPlan.displayText: Add a check before each production stage that blocks deployments outside the approved window, on blocked dates and while customer-facing alarms are in ALARM, and document how an urgent fix overrides it with an audit record. Give the blocked-date calendar an owner and keep it current.

questions.description: Maximum risk: High (launch-blocking unless remediated or formally accepted). Category: Deployment safety. choices.title: Deployments of code, infrastructure, configuration and flags stop and roll back automatically when alarms fire

helpfulResource.displayText: Good looks like: Every deployment path watches alarms during and after each stage and, when one fires, stops promotion and returns to the last known-good version without waiting for a human decision. Platform notes: EC2: AWS CodeDeploy automatic rollback on alarms, or EC2 Auto Scaling instance refresh with automatic rollback. Containers: the Amazon ECS deployment circuit breaker with CloudWatch alarms, or ECS blue/green, linear or canary deployments with bake time. Serverless: Lambda aliases with CodeDeploy traffic shifting and alarms. Infrastructure: CloudFormation rollback triggers. Configuration and flags: AWS AppConfig deployment strategies with alarm-based rollback. CI/CD: CodePipeline stage rollback. improvementPlan.displayText: Pick the native rollback mechanism for each deployment path, wire it to the alarms that represent customer impact, and prove that a deliberately bad change rolls back with no human action. Manual-only rollback is a launch-blocking gap unless the accountable owner formally accepts it, for example for commercial software you cannot redeploy.

choices.title: Rollback alarms use customer-experience, canary and new-version metrics

helpfulResource.displayText: Good looks like: The alarms that trigger rollback measure what customers experience (error rates and latency percentiles), include canary results, and where possible isolate the new version, for example with per-deployment-group or per-version metrics, so a regression shows before it reaches all traffic. How long each stage bakes against these alarms is scored in releases_phased_rollout (pd_bake_time).

improvementPlan.displayText: For each pipeline stage, list the rollback alarms and their evaluation windows, add customer-facing and canary alarms where missing, and add a version dimension to key metrics so the new version can be told apart from the old one.

choices.title: Data-format, protocol and schema changes are backward compatible (readers before writers, expand then contract) and tested

helpfulResource.displayText: Good looks like: Any change that alters data written to storage, caches, queues or the wire can be rolled back without corrupting or stranding data: readers that understand the new format deploy before writers start producing it, and destructive schema steps run only after the old version is gone. Rollback of each such change is tested in pre-production.

improvementPlan.displayText: Adopt a two-phase (prepare, then activate) pattern for format and schema changes, add a pipeline test that deploys version N+1, writes data, rolls back to N and verifies that N can read it, and document the rules for destructive migrations.

choices.title: A one-step rollback to the last known-good release, including configuration, was exercised in the last 12 months

helpfulResource.displayText: Good looks like: In the last 12 months the team performed a rollback, planned or real, of code and configuration in production or a production-like environment with one action, knows how long it takes, and keeps a runbook for the cases where automation does not trigger. The Well-Architected Framework (OPS06-BP01) asks that a rollback plan be documented and tested before deployment so that the time to revert a change is minimized.

improvementPlan.displayText: At least once a year, and ideally each quarter and after pipeline changes, run a planned rollback drill: deploy a harmless change, roll it back with the documented single action, time it, and remove any manual step you needed.

questions.title: Security launch gate: testing, detection and incident readiness
questions.description: Maximum risk: High (launch-blocking unless remediated or formally accepted). Category: Security readiness. Has this release passed security testing with its serious findings closed, and will security events in its accounts reach a responder who has practiced the response? Evidence to collect: the threat model and its last update. The security or penetration test report for this release, with each finding's status. The Regions in use and the detection services enabled in each. The rule that routes findings to on-call. The last security incident exercise report. The log archive account, its retention settings and access policy.

helpfulResource.displayText: SEC11-BP03 Penetration testing (AWS Well-Architected)

choices.title: The threat model and security testing are current for this release, and critical or high findings are fixed or accepted

helpfulResource.displayText: Good looks like: A threat model covers this release's architecture, data flows and trust boundaries, and was updated for the changes in it. Security testing in proportion to the risk, for example penetration testing, dynamic scanning or a focused review of new interfaces, ran against this release or a production-like copy. Every critical and high finding is fixed and retested, or formally accepted by the accountable owner with an expiry date. Testing of AWS resources follows the AWS penetration testing policy.

improvementPlan.displayText: Update the threat model for this release, plan security testing for the new or changed attack surface, run it against a production-like environment within the AWS penetration testing policy, and track every finding to closure. Before launch, fix and retest critical and high findings, or record a time-bound acceptance in your risk register. Reader note: The Threat Composer page mentions Amazon CodeCatalyst, which is closed to new customers; Threat Composer works without it.

content.displayText: Threat Composer (open-source threat modeling tool from AWS)

choices.title: Threat detection and posture findings are enabled in every Region used and routed to an owned on-call queue

helpfulResource.displayText: Good looks like: Threat detection and posture management (for example Amazon GuardDuty and AWS Security Hub) run in every account and every Region the workload uses, including recovery Regions, managed from a delegated administrator account. Findings at or above an agreed severity reach an owned on-call queue within minutes, for example through Amazon EventBridge rules, and the route was tested. Platform notes: EC2 and containers: add GuardDuty Runtime Monitoring and Amazon Inspector scanning. Serverless: add GuardDuty Lambda Protection and Inspector scanning of Lambda functions. Partition notes: GuardDuty, Security Hub, Security Hub CSPM and Inspector are available in AWS GovCloud (US) as of 2026-10-06. There, Security Hub has no third-party integrations and Security Hub CSPM supports only some integrations; route findings with EventBridge. Reader note: This page refers to AWS CloudTrail Lake, which is closed to new customers; a CloudTrail trail to Amazon S3 or CloudWatch Logs meets this practice.

improvementPlan.displayText: Enable threat detection and posture findings organization-wide through a delegated administrator, in every Region the workload uses, and restrict unused Regions, for example with service control policies. Add rules that send findings at or above an agreed severity to the owning team's on-call queue, with a runbook per finding type, and generate sample findings to prove the route works.

choices.title: Security incident playbooks (credential compromise, ransomware, data exposure) were exercised in the last 12 months

helpfulResource.displayText: Good looks like: Playbooks exist for the security incidents most likely to harm this workload, at least credential compromise, ransomware or destructive deletion, and exposure of sensitive data. Each names who decides and who acts, and how to contain, preserve evidence, recover and notify. Each was exercised in the last 12 months as a tabletop or simulation with the people who would respond, including any operations partner under contract, and the gaps found were tracked to closure.

improvementPlan.displayText: Write or adapt playbooks for credential compromise, ransomware and data exposure, run a tabletop exercise on one of them each quarter with the on-call, security and business contacts, and track each gap to closure. Rotate scenarios so that every playbook is exercised at least once a year.

choices.title: Audit and workload logs are centralized in a restricted account, tamper-resistant, and retained to the applicable mandate

helpfulResource.displayText: Good looks like: AWS CloudTrail (an organization trail for all accounts and Regions) and the network, load balancer and application logs that investigations need are delivered to a dedicated log archive account that workload teams cannot change. Log files are protected against change or deletion, for example with S3 Object Lock and CloudTrail log file integrity validation, read access is restricted and audited, and retention meets the longest applicable legal, regulatory or contractual mandate. Partition notes: In AWS GovCloud (US), CloudTrail records events from global services such as IAM and AWS STS in AWS GovCloud (US-West); use a multi-Region trail to capture them (as of 2026-10-06). Reader note: This page refers to AWS CloudTrail Lake, which is closed to new customers; a CloudTrail organization trail to Amazon S3 meets this practice.

improvementPlan.displayText: Create an organization trail into a log archive account, add the other log sources investigations need, turn on log file integrity validation and write-once protection such as S3 Object Lock, restrict read access to the security team with audited access, and set retention per mandate. Confirm in an exercise that a responder can query recent logs quickly.

questions.title: Dependency inventory, classification and partition availability
questions.description: Maximum risk: Medium (not launch-blocking, remediate on a plan). Category: Defense against dependencies. Do you know every dependency of the workload, how critical each one is, and whether each one is available and authorized in every partition and Region you use? Evidence to collect: the dependency inventory with owner, Regions and criticality for each entry. The documented customer impact and degraded behavior for each hard dependency. The dated availability and authorization check for each target partition and Region.

helpfulResource.displayText: AWS Fault Isolation Boundaries: Global services (whitepaper)

choices.title: Every dependency is listed: AWS services by Region (including global), identity, DNS, CI/CD, artifact sources, third parties

helpfulResource.displayText: Good looks like: A maintained inventory lists everything the workload needs to run, deploy and recover: each AWS service and the Regions it is used in, including partitional and global services whose control planes are in one Region (for example IAM, Route 53 public DNS and Amazon CloudFront), identity providers, DNS, certificate authorities, CI/CD tooling, artifact and image sources, and third-party APIs and SaaS. Each entry has an owner, says whether it is used at runtime, at deploy time or only during recovery, and is updated when the architecture changes. Runtime views such as the CloudWatch application map help find dependencies that documents miss. Platform notes: EC2: include AMI sources, configuration management and patch repositories. Containers: include image registries, cluster add-ons and the cluster control plane. Serverless: include event sources, layers and VPC networking such as NAT gateways or interface endpoints.

improvementPlan.displayText: Build the inventory from architecture diagrams, IaC templates, IAM policies, network flow logs and trace maps, then confirm it with the team. Record each dependency's owner, Regions, and whether it is needed at runtime, at deploy time or only during recovery. Review the inventory at each ORR and after major architecture changes.

content.displayText: CloudWatch application map (discover runtime dependencies from telemetry)

choices.title: Each dependency is classified hard or soft, with the customer impact of its failure and the degraded behavior documented

helpfulResource.displayText: Good looks like: For each dependency the inventory states whether the workload fails (hard) or keeps working in a degraded way (soft) when the dependency is slow or unavailable, which customer journeys are affected and how, and the intended degraded behavior (for example serve cached data, queue writes, or turn off a feature). The classification matches what tests or past incidents showed. The behavior itself is scored in this lens's dependency failure handling, retry and restart questions; this statement checks that the classification exists.

improvementPlan.displayText: Walk each critical journey and mark every dependency hard or soft, with the customer impact of its failure and the intended degraded behavior. Confirm the classification with a test or fault injection where you can, and record each hard dependency that should become soft as a tracked backlog item.

choices.title: Every service and feature relied on, including readiness tooling, is verified available and authorized in each target partition

helpfulResource.displayText: Good looks like: Before launch, someone checked every AWS service, feature, API and CloudFormation resource type the workload and its operations rely on, including monitoring, deployment, backup and resilience-testing tools, against current availability in each target Region and partition, and against the compliance authorizations the workload needs (for example FedRAMP or DoD SRG). The check is dated, it is repeated before each launch, and every gap has a documented alternative. Partition notes: Feature availability in AWS GovCloud (US) can differ even when the service is available. For example, as of 2026-10-06 the AWS GovCloud (US) User Guide lists CloudWatch dashboard sharing, CloudWatch Logs Live Tail and Lambda JSON log formatting as not available there, and for CloudWatch Transaction Search it disagrees with AWS Capabilities by Region, so check both and test in your account. Check the per-service pages of that guide and AWS Capabilities by Region; verify per Region.

improvementPlan.displayText: List every service and feature from the inventory and check each one against AWS Capabilities by Region and, for AWS GovCloud (US), the service pages of the GovCloud User Guide. Check the compliance programs you need on AWS Services in Scope by Compliance Program. Record the date and result, design an alternative for anything missing, and repeat the check before each launch and at each recurring review.

questions.title: Customer-experience SLOs and alarms that fire before breach
questions.description: Maximum risk: High (launch-blocking unless remediated or formally accepted). Category: Event detection. Do SLO-based alarms on customer-facing errors and latency page your team before customers notice, and before any SLO or contractual SLA is breached? Evidence to collect: the SLOs for each critical journey and API. The paging alarm definitions (metric, statistic, threshold, period, datapoints to alarm, missing-data treatment). The record of the last operations review with SLO attainment and alarm noise.

helpfulResource.displayText: OPS04-BP01 Identify KPIs (AWS Well-Architected)

choices.title: Availability, latency and async-completion SLOs are defined for each critical user journey and API

helpfulResource.displayText: Good looks like: Each critical user journey and API has written SLOs measured from the customer's side: availability (successful requests over valid requests), latency at a high percentile (for example p99), and, for asynchronous work, time to completion. Each SLO has an owner, a target, a measurement window and an error budget, is derived from business needs, and is tighter than any SLA. CloudWatch Application Signals can track latency and availability SLOs, or you can compute them from your own metrics. Partition notes: As of 2026-10-06, CloudWatch Application Signals is available in AWS GovCloud (US) (AWS Capabilities by Region) but not for Lambda functions (AWS GovCloud (US) User Guide); compute Lambda SLOs from your own CloudWatch metrics. Verify per Region. Reader note: This page mentions AWS Service Catalog AppRegistry, which is closed to new customers; associating an SLO with an application there is optional and is not needed for this practice.

improvementPlan.displayText: For each critical journey and API, agree availability, latency-percentile and completion-time targets with the business owner, set them tighter than any SLA, choose the metric that measures each one from the customer's side, and publish them with an owner and an error budget.

choices.title: Paging alarms on customer-facing error rates and latency percentiles fire before the SLO or SLA is breached

helpfulResource.displayText: Good looks like: Every SLO has at least one alarm that pages the on-call engineer when the error rate or latency percentile crosses a threshold, or the error budget burns at a rate, that leaves time to act before the SLO or SLA is breached. Alarms use rates and percentiles (for example server errors over requests, p99 latency) rather than averages or raw counts, and cover each Region and entry point. Informational alarms go to a ticket queue, not a pager. Platform notes: EC2 and containers behind a load balancer: Application Load Balancer metrics such as HTTPCode_Target_5XX_Count and TargetResponseTime, with metric math for rates. Serverless: API Gateway 5XXError and Latency, and Lambda Errors and Duration. Asynchronous journeys: alarm on completion time or success rate, not only on API errors. Reader note: This page refers to Amazon DevOps Guru (closed to new customers from 2026-10-29, end of support 2027-09-30); CloudWatch alarms, composite alarms and CloudWatch anomaly detection meet this practice.

improvementPlan.displayText: Create an alarm for each SLO on error rate and on latency percentile, with thresholds that fire while error budget remains; consider a fast-burn and a slow-burn alarm per SLO. Route them to the paging rotation, test each one by setting it to ALARM, and keep alarm definitions in IaC.

content.displayText: REL06-BP03 Send notifications (Real-time processing and alarming)

choices.title: Critical alarms use short periods (for example 1 minute), deliberate missing-data handling and M-of-N evaluation

helpfulResource.displayText: Good looks like: Critical alarms evaluate short periods (for example 1 minute) so they fire within minutes, use M out of N datapoints to alarm (for example 3 of 5) so a single spike does not page, and set missing-data treatment on purpose: breaching for signals that must always report, such as request-count or success metrics that should never drop to zero (canary and heartbeat alarms are scored in event_canary_alarms), and not breaching or ignore where gaps are normal. Composite alarms or anomaly detection reduce noise where static thresholds do not fit.

improvementPlan.displayText: Review every paging alarm's period, datapoints to alarm and missing-data treatment, record the reason for each choice, fix alarms that page on a single datapoint or stay quiet when data stops, and check these settings in code review of the alarm IaC.

content.displayText: Related AWS Post-Event Summary (Nov 2020): CloudWatch saw increased error rates and latencies for metric and log ingestion and alarms transitioned to the INSUFFICIENT_DATA state, so decide deliberately how each critical alarm treats missing data.
Using CloudWatch anomaly detection

choices.title: SLO attainment, error budgets and noisy alarms are reviewed in a recurring operations review and drive fixes

helpfulResource.displayText: Good looks like: A weekly or other regular operations review looks at SLO attainment and error budget burn, alarms that fired without needing action or failed to fire, recent pages and open action items, and turns findings into tracked fixes to thresholds, runbooks or the workload. Attendance includes the people who are on call. A sample agenda is in docs/ops-review-agenda.md in this lens's repository.

improvementPlan.displayText: Schedule a recurring operations review with a fixed agenda: SLO attainment and error budget, alarms that fired and whether they were actionable, missed detections, and open action items. Give each fix an owner and a due date and track it to closure.

questions.title: Independent outside-in monitoring of critical journeys
questions.description: Maximum risk: High (launch-blocking unless remediated or formally accepted). Category: Event detection. Do synthetic canaries continuously exercise your critical journeys from the outside, with their own alarms, so you detect customer impact even when internal metrics are missing or misleading? Evidence to collect: the list of critical APIs and journeys mapped to canaries. Canary schedules, Regions and endpoints. Alarm definitions on canary metrics, including missing-data treatment. The accounts and Regions where canaries and their alarms run.

helpfulResource.displayText: OPS04-BP03 User experience telemetry (AWS Well-Architected)

choices.title: Synthetic canaries exercise every critical API and user journey, including async, through customer endpoints in every Region

helpfulResource.displayText: Good looks like: Canaries run every 1 to 5 minutes against the same public or private endpoints customers use, in every Region and entry point, and cover each critical API and journey, including multi-step browser flows and asynchronous work (for example submit a job and check it completes within its SLO). They exercise deep paths that touch data stores and dependencies, not only a health check, use dedicated test accounts or tenants, and are updated when journeys change. Platform notes: Private APIs: run canaries inside the VPC. Asynchronous and event-driven journeys: the canary publishes a test event or message and polls for the result. Partition notes: CloudWatch Synthetics is available in AWS GovCloud (US) as of 2026-10-06 (AWS Capabilities by Region); verify per Region.

improvementPlan.displayText: Map each critical API and journey to a canary, start from a canary blueprint (for example API canary or multi checks for APIs, and GUI workflow builder or canary recorder for browser flows), run it in every Region and entry point every 1 to 5 minutes, and make canary updates part of the definition of done for journey changes.

content.displayText: CloudWatch RUM (optional real-user monitoring for browser clients)

choices.title: Canary success and latency publish their own metrics, with alarms on failure, latency and missing canary data

helpfulResource.displayText: Good looks like: Each canary publishes its own success and duration metrics (CloudWatch Synthetics publishes SuccessPercent and Duration for each canary), separate from service-wide error metrics. Paging alarms fire on canary failures, on latency above the SLO, and when canary data stops arriving (missing data treated as breaching), and a failing canary is detected within minutes (the whitepaper example asks for under five minutes). The AWS ORR whitepaper's example questions treat not publishing canary errors to an independent metric with an alarm as high risk.

improvementPlan.displayText: Create alarms on SuccessPercent and Duration for every canary, with missing data treated as breaching, route them to the paging rotation, and test them by breaking a canary in pre-production. Confirm that a canary failure is detected within your target, for example five minutes.

content.displayText: Configuring how CloudWatch alarms treat missing data

choices.title: Canaries and critical alarms keep working if the workload's account, stack, Region or central monitoring account is impaired

helpfulResource.displayText: Good looks like: Canaries, their alarms and the notification path are deployed separately from the workload (for example in a different account and stack that workload deployments cannot change), and at least one canary checks each Region's customer endpoints from another Region. An impaired workload account, Region or central monitoring account therefore does not also silence detection. A heartbeat alarm, with missing data treated as breaching, shows when the monitoring path itself stops.

improvementPlan.displayText: Move canaries and their alarms to a separate monitoring account and stack, add a cross-Region canary for each Region's customer endpoints, send critical notifications through a path that does not depend on the workload's Region, and add a heartbeat alarm that pages when canary data stops.

content.displayText: Related AWS Post-Event Summary (Dec 2021): customers were impacted by CloudWatch monitoring delays and found it difficult to understand impact to their applications, so keep an outside-in signal that does not depend on the impaired Region.

questions.title: Saturation, dependency health, backlog and usage alarms
questions.description: Maximum risk: High (launch-blocking unless remediated or formally accepted). Category: Event detection. Do alarms warn you about resource exhaustion, dependency degradation, growing backlogs and runaway usage before they turn into customer-facing errors? Evidence to collect: alarm definitions for compute, runtime, data store and dependency metrics. How new resources get alarms. Queue and stream age alarms. Usage-rate alarms. Cost anomaly monitors and their subscribers.

choices.title: Compute or function saturation (CPU, memory, disk, handles, pools, concurrency, throttles) is alarmed and covers new resources

helpfulResource.displayText: Good looks like: Alarms watch the resources that run out first for each compute type, with thresholds that leave time to act: CPU, memory, disk space and inodes, file descriptors, thread and connection pools, runtime signals such as garbage collection, and concurrency and throttling for managed compute. Alarms are created by IaC or tag-driven automation, so new instances, clusters and functions are covered without manual steps. Platform notes: EC2: the CloudWatch agent collects memory, disk and process metrics that EC2 does not publish by default, and JVM workloads can publish JMX metrics. Containers: CloudWatch Container Insights for task, pod and node CPU and memory. Serverless: Lambda Throttles, ConcurrentExecutions and Duration against the timeout, and Lambda Insights for memory. Reader note: This page refers to Amazon DevOps Guru (closed to new customers from 2026-10-29, end of support 2027-09-30); CloudWatch alarms and CloudWatch anomaly detection meet this practice.

improvementPlan.displayText: List the saturation signals for each compute type in the workload, add alarms with headroom thresholds through IaC or automation that runs when resources are created, and check coverage at each ORR by comparing alarmed resources with the resource inventory.

choices.title: Data stores and critical dependencies are alarmed on errors, throttling, latency and capacity headroom, measured from your side

helpfulResource.displayText: Good looks like: Each data store and critical dependency, including AWS services, internal services and third-party APIs, has alarms on the errors, throttles, latency and timeouts your code sees when it calls it, measured with client-side metrics, plus provider metrics for capacity headroom such as connections, storage, read and write capacity or replica lag. The operational dashboard has a view of critical dependencies, so responders can tell quickly whether a problem is in the workload or in a dependency. Platform notes: Managed databases: alarm on connections, storage, CPU and replica lag (for example Amazon RDS and Amazon Aurora metrics). Amazon DynamoDB: alarm on throttled requests and system errors. Third parties: emit your own call metrics from each client, because the provider's metrics are not visible to you. Reader note: This page refers to Amazon DevOps Guru (closed to new customers from 2026-10-29, end of support 2027-09-30); CloudWatch alarms on your own dependency metrics meet this practice.

improvementPlan.displayText: Instrument each dependency client to emit latency, error, throttle and timeout metrics per dependency and operation (for example with the CloudWatch embedded metric format), add alarms on those metrics and on provider capacity metrics, and add a critical-dependencies view to the operational dashboard.

choices.title: Queues and streams alarm on oldest-item age, dead-letter arrivals and completion or replication lag (or none are used)

helpfulResource.displayText: Good looks like: Every queue, stream and asynchronous workflow has alarms on the age of the oldest unprocessed item compared with its completion SLO, on any message arriving in a dead-letter queue, and on end-to-end completion or replication lag, rather than on queue depth alone. Select this also if the workload uses no queues, streams or asynchronous replication. Platform notes: Amazon SQS: ApproximateAgeOfOldestMessage, and ApproximateNumberOfMessagesVisible on the dead-letter queue. Kinesis Data Streams: GetRecords.IteratorAgeMilliseconds. Lambda: IteratorAge for stream event sources and AsyncEventAge for asynchronous invocations. Replicated data: the data store's replica or replication lag metric.

improvementPlan.displayText: For each queue and stream, set an age threshold from its completion SLO, alarm on oldest-item age and on dead-letter arrivals, and alarm on replication lag for replicated data. Document in the runbook how to drain or redrive a backlog safely.

choices.title: Usage-rate alarms reach the owning team within minutes, and cost anomaly alerts within a day

helpfulResource.displayText: Good looks like: Alarms on usage rates (requests, invocations, records processed, egress) catch runaway loops, retry storms and abuse within minutes. AWS Cost Anomaly Detection monitors, with alert subscriptions for the owning team, add a slower spend signal: it runs about three times a day on processed billing data and can take up to 24 hours to detect an anomaly. Quota headroom alarms are scored in architecture_demand_estimates (dem_quota_headroom). Partition notes: Billing and usage reports for AWS GovCloud (US) accounts are viewed from the associated standard account in the commercial partition (AWS GovCloud (US) User Guide, checked 2026-10-06), so set up cost monitoring there and confirm it covers the GovCloud usage. CloudWatch alarms are available in AWS GovCloud (US) as of 2026-10-06; verify per Region.

improvementPlan.displayText: Add alarms on usage-rate metrics for each entry point and consumer, create Cost Anomaly Detection monitors for the workload's accounts or cost allocation tags, subscribe the owning team, and test that alerts reach that team.

questions.title: Request correlation, tracing and automated diagnostics
questions.description: Maximum risk: High (launch-blocking unless remediated or formally accepted). Category: Forensics. When something fails, can responders follow a single request across components, and do alarms give them the data they need to diagnose the problem quickly? Evidence to collect: a sample log line from each component showing the request or trace ID. An error response that returns the ID. The saved queries used in incidents. A trace that crosses an asynchronous hop. The diagnostics an alarm links to or collects.

helpfulResource.displayText: OPS04-BP02 Application telemetry (AWS Well-Architected)

choices.title: Structured logs carry request or trace IDs, appear in error responses, and are centrally queryable during incidents

helpfulResource.displayText: Good looks like: Every component writes structured (for example JSON) logs with a timestamp, the request or trace ID, the caller or tenant, the operation, the outcome and the latency, and passes the ID to downstream calls and messages. Error responses return the request ID. Logs from all components, accounts and Regions are retained and queryable from one place within minutes (for example with CloudWatch Logs Insights), and responders know the saved queries. Logs hold no secrets, credentials or personal data beyond an opaque caller or tenant ID, and sensitive fields are masked. Platform notes: EC2 and containers: ship logs with the CloudWatch agent, the awslogs log driver or Fluent Bit. Serverless: Lambda can emit JSON logs, and Powertools for AWS Lambda adds correlation IDs. API Gateway: log and return the request ID. Partition notes: Lambda JSON log formatting is not available in AWS GovCloud (US) as of 2026-10-06; write JSON from function code instead, for example with the Powertools for AWS Lambda Logger.

improvementPlan.displayText: Adopt one structured log schema with a required request or trace ID, propagate the ID through every call and message, return it in error responses, centralize logs from all accounts and Regions, and save the incident queries responders need. Keep secrets and personal data out of logs, and mask sensitive fields, for example with CloudWatch Logs data protection policies. Test it by tracing one request end to end from a sample error response.

choices.title: Requests are traced across components, including async hops, with open-standard instrumentation (for example OpenTelemetry)

helpfulResource.displayText: Good looks like: Services use OpenTelemetry instrumentation (for example the AWS Distro for OpenTelemetry), propagate trace context through synchronous calls, queues, streams and events, and send traces to a backend such as AWS X-Ray, with sampling that keeps errors and slow requests. Responders can open the trace for a request ID from a log line or an error response. Platform notes: EC2 and containers: run an OpenTelemetry Collector or the CloudWatch agent on the host, as a sidecar or as a daemon set. Serverless: the AWS Distro for OpenTelemetry Lambda layer or Lambda active tracing. Partition notes: As of 2026-10-06, AWS X-Ray is available in AWS GovCloud (US). For CloudWatch Transaction Search and the OTLP endpoint, the AWS GovCloud (US) User Guide says not available but AWS Capabilities by Region says available; test in your account first. Reader note: The linked support timeline covers the AWS X-Ray SDKs and daemon, in maintenance mode since 2026-02-25; use OpenTelemetry for new instrumentation.

improvementPlan.displayText: Instrument each service with OpenTelemetry, starting with automatic instrumentation, propagate context through messaging, choose a sampling policy that keeps errors, and send traces to your tracing backend. Move existing instrumentation built on maintenance-mode tracing SDKs to OpenTelemetry.

choices.title: Alarms link to dashboards, saved queries and recent changes, and diagnostics are gathered automatically when they fire

helpfulResource.displayText: Good looks like: Each paging alarm's description or ticket links to the dashboard, saved log queries and traces for the affected component, and to recent deployments and configuration changes. When the alarm fires, automation collects the first diagnostics (for example top errors, affected hosts or tenants, recent change events, and thread dumps where safe) and attaches them to the ticket, so responders start with evidence instead of gathering it. Platform notes: An Amazon EventBridge rule on alarm state changes, or an alarm action, can start an AWS Lambda function or an AWS Systems Manager Automation runbook that gathers data. Any incident or ticketing tool can hold the results. Reader note: This page refers to Amazon DevOps Guru (closed to new customers from 2026-10-29, end of support 2027-09-30); alarm actions, Amazon EventBridge rules and Systems Manager Automation runbooks meet this practice.

improvementPlan.displayText: Add links to dashboards, saved queries and the change log to every paging alarm description, then automate the first diagnostic steps of your most frequent runbooks so they run when the alarm fires and post the results to the incident ticket or channel.

questions.title: On-call paging, runbooks and escalation
questions.description: Maximum risk: High (launch-blocking unless remediated or formally accepted). Category: Escalation. When a critical alarm fires, is a trained person paged at every hour the workload must be available, do they have a runbook for that alarm, and does the page escalate if nobody responds? Evidence to collect: the on-call schedule and its coverage hours. Page acknowledgment times for the last quarter. The alarm-to-runbook mapping. The date each runbook was last exercised. Escalation policies and contact paths.

helpfulResource.displayText: OPS07-BP01 Ensure personnel capability (AWS Well-Architected)

choices.title: Critical alarms page a trained on-call rotation, in-house or contracted, for all hours the workload must be available

helpfulResource.displayText: Good looks like: Every paging alarm notifies a named rotation through a paging tool that confirms delivery and acknowledgment, during every hour the workload's documented availability requires (not 24x7 by default). On-call engineers are trained on the workload and have the access they need before their shift starts. Time to acknowledge has a target (for example 5 to 15 minutes for critical pages) and is tracked. The rotation may be in-house or provided by an operations partner under contract, with evidence you can inspect.

improvementPlan.displayText: Define the hours the workload must be supported, staff a rotation with enough trained people to cover them sustainably, connect paging alarms to a paging tool (for example through Amazon SNS to a partner paging service), set and track an acknowledgment target, and send a test page whenever the rotation changes.

choices.title: Every paging alarm links to a runbook from the alarm or the ticket

helpfulResource.displayText: Good looks like: Each paging alarm's description, or the ticket it creates, links to a runbook for that alarm: what the alarm means, how to check customer impact, the first mitigation steps (for example roll back, shift traffic or add capacity), the permissions needed, and when to escalate. An alarm without a runbook does not page, and new paging alarms are reviewed for a runbook before they go live. Reader note: This page refers to AWS Systems Manager Incident Manager, which is closed to new customers; any incident-management or paging tool, or a runbook link in the alarm description, meets this practice.

improvementPlan.displayText: Inventory paging alarms, write a short runbook for each one (starting with the most frequent), put the runbook link in the alarm description, and add a check to alarm code review or CI that fails when a paging alarm has no runbook link. Automate stable runbook steps where it is safe.

choices.title: Runbooks, including the permissions they need, were exercised in the last 12 months or after major changes

helpfulResource.displayText: Good looks like: Each runbook was run end to end in the last 12 months, or since the last major change, by someone other than its author, in a game day, a pre-production drill or a real event, using the same roles and permissions on-call engineers have. Steps that failed, were unclear or needed missing access were fixed, and the runbook records the date it was last exercised. Reader note: This page links to an example that uses AWS CloudTrail Lake, which is closed to new customers; any runbook format or tool meets this practice.

improvementPlan.displayText: Add a last-exercised date to each runbook, schedule drills for runbooks older than 12 months or affected by major changes, run them with on-call roles and permissions, and fix what failed. Combine drills with your game days where possible.

choices.title: Unacknowledged pages escalate automatically, and incident-lead, management, security and dependency-owner paths are documented

helpfulResource.displayText: Good looks like: The paging tool escalates a page that is not acknowledged within the target to a secondary responder and then to a manager. Documented paths say when and how to engage an incident lead, management, the security team and internal dependency owners, with contacts kept current. Escalation to AWS and other providers is scored in event_provider_escalation, and reaching contacts when normal tools are down is scored in event_emergency_access. Reader note: This page refers to AWS Systems Manager Incident Manager, which is closed to new customers; any paging or incident-management tool with escalation policies meets this practice.

improvementPlan.displayText: Configure an escalation policy in your paging tool (primary, secondary, manager), test it by leaving a test page unacknowledged, and document escalation paths and contacts for incident command, management, security and internal dependency owners. Review the contacts at each rotation change.

questions.title: Escalation to AWS and other providers, and provider-initiated change
questions.description: Maximum risk: High (launch-blocking unless remediated or formally accepted). Category: Escalation. Can you engage AWS and your other providers quickly during an event, even when their consoles or support APIs are impaired, and do provider-initiated changes reach you early enough to test them before production? Evidence to collect: the escalation runbook with its fallback contacts and the date it was last tested. The support arrangement and target initial-response time for each production account compared with the workload RTO. The routing rules for AWS Health events and third-party status feeds and the queue they reach. The last provider-initiated change and where it was tested first.

helpfulResource.displayText: OPS10-BP04 Define escalation paths (AWS Well-Architected)

choices.title: A tested runbook escalates to AWS and other providers, with fallbacks that do not depend on the Support Center console or API

helpfulResource.displayText: Good looks like: A runbook says when and how to open and escalate a case with AWS and each critical third-party provider: severity, account, Region and resource details, who may escalate, and response commitments. Fallbacks do not depend on the AWS Support Center console or API (for example account team contacts, if your support includes them, or a contracted operations partner), and provider contacts and contract IDs are reachable during the event. In the last 12 months contacts were confirmed and each fallback was used once (such as a low-severity test case); exercise rehearsal is scored in event_gameday. Partition notes: AWS GovCloud (US), as of 2026-10-06: open cases in the GovCloud Support Center with GovCloud credentials, choose severity carefully (it cannot be changed later), confirm partner fallbacks can manage GovCloud cases, and keep export-controlled data out of cases. Reader note: This page names AWS Systems Manager Incident Manager, closed to new customers; any paging tool meets this practice.

improvementPlan.displayText: For AWS and each critical provider, document how to open and escalate a case, your severity definitions, the details to include, approvers and contacts. Add at least one fallback that works when the AWS Support Center console and API are impaired, store the runbook and contacts where responders can reach them during a Regional or identity outage, link the runbook from your paging runbooks, and verify each fallback path once a year.

content.displayText: Related AWS Post-Event Summary (Oct 2025): customers were unable to create, view and update support cases through the AWS Support Console and API for almost three hours, so keep an escalation fallback that does not depend on them.
AWS Support in AWS GovCloud (US)

choices.title: Each production account has a support arrangement whose target initial-response time fits the workload's RTO

helpfulResource.displayText: Good looks like: For each production account, including accounts that host shared networking, identity and logging, you know which support arrangement covers it, its target initial-response time for your most severe case type, and how that compares with the workload's recovery time objective (RTO). Where the target is too slow for the RTO, the gap is closed or accepted in writing. The arrangement may be an AWS Support plan, a reseller or partner support agreement, or both; the lens compares response targets, not plan names. Partition notes: As of 2026-10-06 the AWS Support Plans page states that Developer, Business and Enterprise On-Ramp Support remain available in AWS GovCloud (US), so plans for GovCloud accounts can differ from those for commercial accounts; check the plan and response targets for each GovCloud account.

improvementPlan.displayText: List every production account and the support arrangement that covers it, record the target initial-response time for production-down cases, compare it with the RTO of the workloads in that account, and close or formally accept each gap. Re-check after account moves, plan or contract changes and RTO changes.

choices.title: AWS Health events, including planned lifecycle notices, and third-party status feeds reach an owned on-call queue

helpfulResource.displayText: Good looks like: AWS Health events for every production account (per account, or aggregated with the AWS Health organizational view) and the status feeds of critical third-party providers create tickets or pages in a queue that a named team watches, with severity mapped by event type. Planned lifecycle events, for example an engine or Kubernetes version reaching end of support or a certificate authority change, become tracked work with an owner and a due date before the provider's deadline. Routing was tested end to end. Partition notes: In AWS GovCloud (US), as of 2026-10-06: the EventBridge channel does not send public events from the Service Health view (use the AWS Health API or the RSS feed), the AWS Health API has a single endpoint in us-gov-west-1, each GovCloud Region is the backup Region for the other, and global events such as IAM events need a rule in AWS GovCloud (US-West).

improvementPlan.displayText: Create Amazon EventBridge rules for AWS Health events in every production account and Region you use, or aggregate events with the AWS Health organizational view and a delegated administrator, and route them to your ticketing or paging tool. Subscribe to the status feeds of critical third-party providers, turn planned lifecycle events into owned work items, and test the routing end to end.

choices.title: Provider-initiated changes (engine, runtime, Kubernetes, certificate authority) are tested in pre-production before production

helpfulResource.displayText: Good looks like: When a provider announces or schedules a change, such as a database engine version reaching end of support, a runtime deprecation, a Kubernetes version upgrade or a certificate authority rotation, you apply it to pre-production first, run your normal tests and a bake period, and then apply it to production ahead of the provider's deadline, so a forced upgrade never reaches production untested. Where the provider applies the change for you, you use the maintenance windows or version controls it offers. Platform notes: EC2: operating system and agent updates through your image pipeline. Containers: Amazon EKS Kubernetes version and add-on upgrades. Serverless: AWS Lambda runtime deprecations and runtime version update controls. Data: Amazon RDS engine versions and certificate authority rotation.

improvementPlan.displayText: Inventory the provider-managed versions you depend on (engines, runtimes, Kubernetes and platform versions, certificate authorities) with their end-of-support dates, link each to the matching AWS Health or provider notice, and schedule every change through pre-production with your normal tests and bake time before production. Pin or control versions where the service allows, and track each deadline as owned work.

questions.title: Identify impacted customers and keep them informed
questions.description: Maximum risk: High (launch-blocking unless remediated or formally accepted). Category: Escalation. During an event, can you quickly tell which customers, tenants or downstream consumers are affected, and keep them informed through a channel that still works? Out of scope if: the workload has no users or downstream consumers to notify (rare). Evidence to collect: saved queries or dashboards that list affected customers. The communication plan and templates. The status channel and its dependencies. The last exercise or event that used them.

helpfulResource.displayText: OPS10-BP05 Customer communication plan (AWS Well-Architected)

choices.title: Telemetry identifies affected users, tenants or downstream consumers within minutes, using queries prepared in advance

helpfulResource.displayText: Good looks like: Request logs and metrics carry a customer, tenant or consumer identifier. Saved queries (for example CloudWatch Logs Insights queries that return every affected customer or tenant) list who saw errors or high latency in a time window, per Region and AZ, within minutes, and CloudWatch Contributor Insights rules show the top contributors and how many unique customers are affected. Results can be shared with the communications team without exposing sensitive data.

improvementPlan.displayText: Add a customer or tenant identifier to structured logs and key metrics, save queries that list affected customers by error type and time window, test them in a game day, and document who may run and share the results.

content.displayText: OPS10-BP03 Prioritize operational events based on business impact (AWS Well-Architected)

choices.title: A communication plan (channels, templates, approvers, cadence, required notices) exists and has been exercised

helpfulResource.displayText: Good looks like: A written plan says who decides to notify, who approves the wording, which channels reach which audiences, how often to update during an event, and which contractual or regulatory notice deadlines apply, with pre-approved templates. In the last 12 months it was used in a real event or an exercise, or each channel and approver was checked, for example with a test notice. Rehearsing communications in an incident exercise is scored in event_gameday (gd_tabletop). Reader note: Some services named on this page are closed to new customers or have an announced end of support (for example AWS Systems Manager Incident Manager, closed to new customers, and Amazon Pinpoint, whose support ends on 2026-10-30). Any incident-management, paging or notification tool meets this practice, for example Amazon SNS, AWS End User Messaging or a partner tool.

improvementPlan.displayText: Write the plan with your communications, legal and customer-support owners, pre-approve templates for common event types, list notice obligations and deadlines, and check each channel and approver at least once a year, for example with a test notice or in your next exercise.

choices.title: Customer status updates use a channel that does not depend on the affected workload or its Region

helpfulResource.displayText: Good looks like: The status page, the notification service and the tools used to publish updates are hosted independently of the workload, its accounts, its identity provider and its primary Region, so you can publish while the workload is down. The fallback publishing path is documented, familiar to the people who use it, and tested.

improvementPlan.displayText: Map the dependencies of your status and notification path, move it to infrastructure that does not share accounts, identity or Region with the workload, or to a separate provider, keep a documented manual fallback, and practice publishing through the fallback in a game day.

content.displayText: Related AWS Post-Event Summary (Nov 2020): status updates were delayed because the usual publishing tool depended on an impaired service and the backup tool was less familiar, so keep the status path independent and practice the fallback.

questions.title: Survive the loss of one Availability Zone without scaling
questions.description: Maximum risk: High (launch-blocking unless remediated or formally accepted). Category: Blast radius containment. If one Availability Zone becomes impaired at peak load, can the workload keep serving customers using only the capacity already running in the other Availability Zones? Out of scope if: never as a whole question. If the critical path uses only Regional managed services, select the first statement and keep the AZ layout as evidence. Evidence to collect: per-AZ capacity compared with peak demand. The AZ layout of every tier, data store and network path. The report of the last AZ-loss test at load.

helpfulResource.displayText: Static stability using Availability Zones (Builders' Library)

choices.title: Only Regional managed services on the critical path: no zonal NAT gateways, single-AZ subnets, instances or databases

helpfulResource.displayText: Good looks like: Every component on the critical path is a Regional service whose AZ resilience AWS manages for you, for example AWS Lambda, Amazon DynamoDB, Amazon S3, Amazon SQS or Amazon API Gateway. Lambda functions attached to a VPC count only if their subnets span at least two AZs and nothing else on the path is zonal, such as zonal NAT gateways, interface endpoints, instances, containers or databases you place in AZs. Evidence to collect: the AZ layout of every network path and data store on the critical path. When this is selected, the other statements do not change the score.

improvementPlan.displayText: Check your component list against the AWS Fault Isolation Boundaries whitepaper. If any customer-managed zonal resource is on the critical path, clear this statement and answer the other statements.

choices.title: Every customer-managed tier spans at least two AZs (three recommended), with no single-AZ or single-instance component

helpfulResource.displayText: Good looks like: Compute, data stores, caches, load balancers, network appliances and every other zonal component run in at least two AZs, with three recommended so that losing one still leaves two. Data is replicated synchronously or within a known RPO, and nothing on the critical path exists in only one AZ or as a single instance. Platform notes: EC2: Auto Scaling groups spanning AZs. Containers: Amazon ECS services or Kubernetes topology spread constraints across AZs. Data: Multi-AZ deployments for managed databases and caches. Network: no single-AZ gateway, appliance or endpoint on the critical path.

improvementPlan.displayText: Inventory the AZ placement of every tier, including data stores and network paths, remove single-AZ and single-instance components or record a formal acceptance, and add a recurring check, for example AWS Config managed rules for Multi-AZ settings, so new single-AZ resources are flagged.

content.displayText: REL10-BP01 Deploy the workload to multiple locations (AWS Well-Architected)

choices.title: Capacity already running in the remaining AZs carries peak load with no scaling or new launches during the event

helpfulResource.displayText: Good looks like: Each AZ runs enough capacity that losing any one AZ leaves the rest able to serve peak load within latency goals (for example, with three AZs each holds at least half of peak), and recovery does not depend on launching instances, tasks or pods, which may be slow or impaired during the same event. Capacity Reservations can hold capacity for critical instance types. The AWS ORR whitepaper's example questions treat not being statically stable to the loss of an AZ as high risk. Platform notes: EC2: per-AZ Auto Scaling minimums and Capacity Reservations. Containers: Amazon ECS desired counts and Kubernetes node groups sized so each AZ already runs its share of peak with headroom, because new task, pod and AWS Fargate launches can also be impaired during the event. Serverless: AWS manages the AZ capacity of AWS Lambda, so size only the zonal components on the path.

improvementPlan.displayText: Calculate the capacity each AZ must hold to absorb the loss of one AZ at peak, provision it (with Capacity Reservations for critical instance types if needed), set Auto Scaling minimums so scale-in cannot remove it, and alarm when capacity in any AZ falls below the target.

content.displayText: AWS ORR whitepaper, Appendix B Example ORR questions (AZ static stability)
Related AWS Post-Event Summary (Oct 2025): new EC2 instance launches failed for hours while existing instances remained healthy, so plan recovery around capacity that is already running.

choices.title: Loss of one AZ was simulated at production-like load in the last 12 months, and recovery did not depend on adding capacity

helpfulResource.displayText: Good looks like: In the last 12 months a fault-injection experiment removed one AZ while production-like load ran (for example the AWS FIS AZ Availability: Power Interruption scenario), customer-facing metrics stayed within goals using existing capacity, and the time to recover and the fixes were recorded. Repeat it after major changes. Partition notes: AWS FIS AZ scenarios are available in AWS GovCloud (US); the FIS experiment scheduling and experiment report features are not (as of 2026-10-06; verify per Region).

improvementPlan.displayText: Plan an AZ-loss experiment with stop conditions on customer-facing alarms. Start in pre-production at production-like load, then move to production with a limited blast radius when you are confident. Record time to detect and recover, and fix anything that needed new capacity. For critical workloads, repeat it at least quarterly or run it in the deployment pipeline (a suggestion).

questions.description: Maximum risk: High (launch-blocking unless remediated or formally accepted). Category: Blast radius containment. If one Availability Zone is impaired, including a partial (gray) failure, can you detect it and move traffic and work away from that Availability Zone within minutes? Out of scope if: never as a whole question. If the critical path uses only Regional managed services, select the first statement and keep the AZ layout as evidence. Evidence to collect: per-AZ dashboards and alarms. The AZ shift runbook or automation and the resources it covers. Detection and mitigation times from the last practice shift or exercise. The AZ layout of every network path and data store on the critical path.

helpfulResource.displayText: REL11-BP01 Monitor all components to detect failures

choices.title: Only Regional managed services on the critical path: no zonal NAT gateways, single-AZ subnets, instances or databases

helpfulResource.displayText: Good looks like: Every component on the critical path is a Regional service whose AZ resilience AWS manages for you, for example AWS Lambda, Amazon DynamoDB, Amazon S3, Amazon SQS or Amazon API Gateway, so there is no zonal capacity of yours to shift. Lambda functions attached to a VPC count only if their subnets span at least two AZs and nothing else on the path is zonal, such as zonal NAT gateways, interface endpoints, instances, containers or databases you place in AZs. Evidence to collect: the AZ layout of every network path and data store on the critical path. When this is selected, the other statements do not change the score.

improvementPlan.displayText: Check your component list against the AWS Fault Isolation Boundaries whitepaper. If any customer-managed zonal resource is on the critical path, clear this statement and answer the other statements.

choices.title: A data-plane mechanism moves traffic and work away from one AZ within minutes (for example ARC zonal shift or zonal autoshift)

helpfulResource.displayText: Good looks like: A runbook or automation takes one AZ out of service within minutes (the AWS ORR whitepaper's example asks for 15) for every zonal path: load-balanced traffic, east-west calls, queue consumers and data store primaries. It uses data-plane actions that keep working during the event, for example Amazon Application Recovery Controller (ARC) zonal shift, or zonal autoshift, where AWS shifts traffic for you when it detects an AZ impairment. Platform notes: EC2: zonal shift supports Auto Scaling groups and Application and Network Load Balancers. Containers: Amazon EKS with zonal shift enabled; Amazon ECS tasks behind a shifted load balancer stop receiving its traffic in that AZ. Serverless: only zonal resources on the path need a shift. Data: database failover is usually a control-plane action, so shift traffic first. Partition notes: ARC zonal shift, zonal autoshift and practice runs are available in AWS GovCloud (US); ARC routing control is not (as of 2026-10-06; verify per Region).

improvementPlan.displayText: Enable zonal shift for every supported resource on the critical path, and write a runbook or automation that also covers what ARC does not shift, such as queue consumers, east-west traffic and data store primaries. Measure how long a full AZ evacuation takes against your target, and consider zonal autoshift once every AZ is pre-scaled to carry the load without the impaired one.

A fault-injection experiment that degraded one AZ only partially, for example the AWS FIS scenarios AZ: Application Slowdown or Cross-AZ: Traffic Slowdown, proved the alarms fire. improvementPlan.displayText: Publish error and latency metrics with an AZ dimension for every zonal tier, alarm when one AZ deviates from the others, and link the alarm to the AZ shift runbook. Then run a partial-AZ experiment with stop conditions in pre-production, and later in production, to prove the alarms fire and identify the AZ.

Each practice records the time from detection to mitigation and compares it with your documented target, and problems found become tracked fixes. Partition notes: ARC practice runs are available in both AWS GovCloud (US) Regions (as of 2026-10-06; verify per Region).

You can combine practice with fault injection, for example by testing zonal autoshift with AWS FIS.

questions.title: Production access: read-only by default, time-bound elevation
questions.description: Maximum risk: High (launch-blocking unless remediated or formally accepted). Category: Operator safety. How do you reduce the chance and the impact of human error and credential misuse when people and automation can change production? Evidence to collect: the roles or permission sets people use in production and their default permissions. The elevation workflow with its approvals and session logs. Root user controls for every account. The last access review and the roles used by pipelines, automation and AI agents.

helpfulResource.displayText: SEC03-BP02 Grant least privilege access (AWS Well-Architected)

choices.title: Human roles are read-only in production by default, and only pipeline and automation roles hold standing write access

helpfulResource.displayText: Good looks like: The roles people use in production every day grant read-only or view-only permissions, and routine operational tasks run through reviewed automation (for example AWS Systems Manager Automation runbooks) rather than ad hoc human changes. Mutating permissions belong to pipeline and automation roles. A person who must change production uses the time-bound elevation path or the emergency path, never a standing administrator role. Pipeline-only deployment of code, infrastructure and configuration is scored in releases_manual_changes. Platform notes: EC2: use AWS Systems Manager Session Manager with session logging instead of SSH keys or bastion hosts, and restrict who can start sessions. Containers: give people read-only Kubernetes permissions, for example with Amazon EKS access entries and access policies, and restrict Amazon ECS Exec. Serverless: read-only roles keep people from editing functions, state machines or API configurations in the console.

improvementPlan.displayText: List the roles and permission sets people use in production, replace standing write access with read-only or view-only defaults (the AWS managed job-function policies ReadOnlyAccess, or ViewOnlyAccess where people should not read data, are starting points), move routine changes into pipelines or reviewed automation, and alarm on mutating API calls made by human roles outside the elevation path.

content.displayText: Manage AWS accounts with permission sets (IAM Identity Center)

choices.title: Human write access is time-bound, approved and session-logged, and people use no long-term access keys for daily work

helpfulResource.displayText: Good looks like: When a person needs write access to production, they request it for a specific task and time, someone else approves it, the access expires automatically, and the session and its API calls are logged and attributable to that person (for example AWS CloudTrail plus session logs). People sign in through federation or IAM Identity Center and use temporary credentials; nobody uses long-term IAM user access keys for daily work. Partition notes: IAM Identity Center is available in both AWS GovCloud (US) Regions (as of 2026-10-06); the administrative console, SDK and CLI use FIPS endpoints there.

improvementPlan.displayText: Choose a temporary elevated access mechanism, for example a validated partner solution that integrates with IAM Identity Center or the open-source TEAM solution, define who may approve elevation and for how long, log every elevated session, and replace IAM users and long-term access keys used by people with federated sign-in and temporary credentials.

content.displayText: Temporary elevated access management (TEAM) for IAM Identity Center (aws-samples)
