choices.title: Root users are locked down (MFA, no access keys, alert on use), and member-account root credentials are removed where possible

helpfulResource.displayText: Good looks like: Every account's root user has MFA, no access keys, recovery contacts that the organization controls, and an alert on any root sign-in or API call. In AWS Organizations member accounts, root user credentials are removed with centralized root access, and tasks that need root run as short-lived privileged sessions from the management account or the delegated administrator for IAM. Partition notes: In AWS GovCloud (US), as of 2026-10-06, access to the root user is not provided by default and console sign-in as root is not available, so there are no root credentials to manage centrally, but privileged tasks on member accounts are available. Protect the root user of the associated standard account, which can request GovCloud root access keys.

improvementPlan.displayText: Enable MFA and delete access keys for every root user, alert on root activity (for example an Amazon EventBridge rule on AWS CloudTrail events for the root user), enable centralized root access for member accounts and remove their root credentials except where a documented emergency path still relies on them, and document who may run privileged root tasks and how each is approved.

choices.title: Privileged sessions are reviewed, access is re-certified, and automation and AI agents use least-privilege roles

helpfulResource.displayText: Good looks like: Elevated and emergency sessions are reviewed after use, standing access is re-certified on a schedule (for example quarterly) by each account's owner, and unused roles and permissions are removed. Pipelines, automation and AI agents that can change production run under their own least-privilege roles, never with a person's credentials, and their actions are logged and attributable.

improvementPlan.displayText: Schedule access reviews with account owners, review every elevated session, use IAM Access Analyzer unused access findings and last-accessed information to remove permissions nobody uses, give each pipeline, automation and AI agent its own scoped role, and keep the review results as evidence.

questions.title: Emergency access that works when normal sign-in fails
questions.description: Maximum risk: High (launch-blocking unless remediated or formally accepted). Category: Operator safety. If your identity provider, your federation configuration or the Region that hosts your sign-in and identity configuration fails during an incident, can responders still reach the AWS accounts and tools they need to mitigate it? Evidence to collect: the emergency access runbook for each failure mode. The emergency account, roles and credential custody records. The date, participants and result of the last test of each path. Where runbooks, the contact roster and the incident bridge are hosted and how people sign in to them.

helpfulResource.displayText: SEC03-BP03 Emergency access process (AWS Well-Architected)

choices.title: Emergency access is defined for each failure mode: identity provider down, sign-in Region impaired, federation broken

helpfulResource.displayText: Good looks like: A documented emergency access process exists for each way sign-in can fail: your external identity provider is unavailable; the AWS-side federation or SAML configuration was changed or its certificate expired; IAM Identity Center or the Region that hosts it is impaired. Each process states when it may and may not be used, who may start it, who approves it (including out of hours, with secondary approvers), which pre-created emergency account and roles it uses, and how its use is logged, alerted and linked to an incident record. Emergency credentials are rotated after each use, and any use outside a declared incident raises an alert.

improvementPlan.displayText: List what responders depend on to sign in (identity provider, IAM Identity Center and its Region, SAML configuration, MFA devices, credential vault) and how each can fail. For each failure mode, write a short runbook with pre-conditions, approvers and steps. Pre-create the emergency account, roles and cross-account trust before you need them (for example with CloudFormation StackSets), protect them with service control policies, and alert on any sign-in or API activity by the emergency roles outside a declared incident.

choices.title: Each emergency path is tested on a schedule, including one that depends on neither your IdP nor the Region hosting identity

helpfulResource.displayText: Good looks like: Every emergency path was used end to end on a schedule (for example every 6 months, a suggestion) and after identity or account changes, by the people who would use it, reaching production accounts with the expected permissions. At least one path depends on neither your identity provider nor the Region that hosts IAM Identity Center, for example IAM users with MFA in a dedicated emergency account that sign in through a Regional sign-in endpoint for another Region, with credentials and MFA devices pre-provisioned and held in a vault responders can reach during an outage. Responder tools use Regional AWS STS endpoints, and federated paths use more than one Regional SAML endpoint. Partition notes: In AWS GovCloud (US), console sign-in as the account root user is not available, so use IAM users with MFA and the AWS GovCloud (US) sign-in endpoints. IAM Identity Center multi-Region replication, including between the AWS GovCloud (US) Regions, is available as of 2026-10-06; verify per Region.

improvementPlan.displayText: Schedule a test of every emergency path, including the independent one. Run it from a clean workstation with only the credentials and devices the runbook names, and record the time to access and every gap. Give each emergency IAM user a Regional console sign-in URL, use that URL in the test, and confirm that the MFA type the user holds works through it: the IAM resilience page warns that Universal 2nd Factor (U2F) MFA might not complete. Configure your identity provider for multiple Regional SAML sign-in endpoints, consider IAM Identity Center multi-Region replication (organization instances with an external identity provider or the Identity Center directory, not Active Directory, and a multi-Region customer managed KMS key) so that access provisioned before a disruption keeps working when the primary Region is impaired, and switch scripts and tools to Regional AWS STS endpoints. Repeat the test after identity, Region or account changes.

choices.title: Runbooks, contact roster and incident bridge stay reachable when your identity provider or primary Region is impaired

helpfulResource.displayText: Good looks like: Responders can open the runbooks, reach the on-call and escalation contacts, and join the incident bridge or chat channel when your identity provider, corporate network or the workload's primary Region is impaired. For example, a current copy of runbooks and contacts is kept outside the affected Region and sign-in path, a dial-in bridge and an out-of-band chat channel (for example AWS Wickr or a partner tool) exist, and each responder holds an offline contact list. The runbook names the fallback channel, and it was used in an exercise. Partition notes: AWS WickrGov, the AWS GovCloud (US) offering of AWS Wickr and one example of an out-of-band channel, is available only in the AWS GovCloud (US-West) Region as of 2026-10-06; verify per Region.

improvementPlan.displayText: List where each incident tool is hosted and how people sign in to it, and remove shared dependencies on your identity provider and the workload's primary Region. Keep a current read-only copy of runbooks and contacts in a second location, set up a fallback bridge and chat channel with independent sign-in, give responders an offline contact list, and switch to the fallbacks during your next game day.

questions.title: Operator tools prevent a mistaken action from causing an outage
questions.description: Maximum risk: High (launch-blocking unless remediated or formally accepted). Category: Operator safety. If an operator enters a wrong input or targets the wrong resource with a runbook command, script or console action, what stops that one action from taking the workload down or deleting critical data? Evidence to collect: the list of operator tools, scripts and runbook commands that change production. Their input validation, rate and scope limits and minimum-capacity checks. Deletion protection and stack policy settings on critical resources. How high-impact commands are previewed or approved.

helpfulResource.displayText: AWS ORR whitepaper Appendix A, guidance from an incident

choices.title: Operator tools and runbook commands validate inputs, cap what one action can change, and refuse to go below minimum capacity

helpfulResource.displayText: Good looks like: Every tool, script or automated runbook that changes production checks its inputs against allowed values or patterns, shows the resolved list of targets, limits how many resources or what percentage of capacity one run can change, acts in small batches with pauses, and stops when error thresholds are crossed. Capacity-removing actions refuse to take any tier below its documented minimum. Operators use these tools rather than ad hoc commands for routine production tasks. Platform notes: EC2: Auto Scaling group minimums and scale-in protection. Containers: minimum healthy percent on Amazon ECS services, pod disruption budgets on Kubernetes. Serverless: reserved concurrency and alias weights are changed only through reviewed automation. Fleet actions: AWS Systems Manager Automation and Run Command concurrency and error thresholds.

improvementPlan.displayText: Inventory the commands operators run in production and wrap the risky ones in automation runbooks with typed, validated parameters (for example allowedValues or allowedPattern in Systems Manager documents), a target preview, concurrency and error-threshold limits, and a minimum-capacity check that aborts the run. Retire direct use of the underlying commands for those tasks, and add the safety checks to every similar tool.

content.displayText: Related AWS Post-Event Summary (Feb 2017): a single incorrect input to an operational command removed a larger set of servers than intended and caused hours of impact, so make operator tools validate inputs, remove capacity in small steps and refuse to take any tier below its minimum capacity.
Use instance scale-in protection to control instance termination (Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling)

choices.title: Critical resources have deletion protection, stack policies or equivalent safeguards

helpfulResource.displayText: Good looks like: Every critical resource whose loss would cause an outage or data loss has a guard that a single mistaken action cannot bypass: deletion protection on databases and tables, termination protection on stacks and critical instances, CloudFormation stack policies and DeletionPolicy or UpdateReplacePolicy set to Retain or Snapshot for stateful resources, and service control policies that deny deleting or modifying protected resources except through an approved role. Turning a guard off is itself a reviewed, logged change. Platform notes: Data: Amazon RDS and Aurora deletion protection, Amazon DynamoDB deletion protection, and bucket policies or service control policies that deny bucket deletion (S3 versioning and Object Lock are scored in architecture_data_corruption). EC2: instance termination protection. Infrastructure as code: stack termination protection, stack policies and retain policies, or the equivalent in your tool.

improvementPlan.displayText: List the resources whose deletion or replacement would cause an outage or data loss. Turn on deletion or termination protection for each, set retain or snapshot policies on stateful resources in your templates, add stack policies for critical resources, and add a service control policy that denies deletes on resources tagged as protected except through a break-glass or pipeline role. Alarm when a protection setting is turned off.

content.displayText: Protect CloudFormation stacks from being deleted (termination protection)

choices.title: High-impact commands support a dry run or require a second person to approve

helpfulResource.displayText: Good looks like: Commands that can remove capacity, delete data, change routing or change access show exactly what they will do before they do it (for example an automation step that lists the resolved targets and waits for confirmation, or a tool flag that only prints the intended actions), and the highest-impact ones need a second person to approve before they run. The approval works out of hours, is recorded with the change, and the emergency path for urgent fixes is logged and reviewed afterward. Previews of infrastructure as code changes are scored in releases_manual_changes.

improvementPlan.displayText: Classify operator commands by impact. For the high-impact ones, add a preview step that prints the intended actions and targets, and an approval step by someone other than the operator, for example the aws:approve action in a Systems Manager Automation runbook or a manual approval action in AWS CodePipeline. Review approval records and emergency bypasses in your operations review. Reader note: the aws:approve page also describes an input used only by AWS Systems Manager Change Manager templates; Change Manager is closed to new customers and is not needed for this practice.

questions.title: Certificates, credentials and other expiring materials
questions.description: Maximum risk: High (launch-blocking unless remediated or formally accepted). Category: Event detection. Could an expired or replaced certificate, certificate authority, key, secret, token or other time-bound material take the workload down, and would the owning team know and act well before it expires? Evidence to collect: the inventory of expiring materials with owner, expiry date and renewal method. The expiry and renewal-failure alarms with their lead times. Client, device and partner trust configuration, including any pinning. The record of the last renewal or rotation of each kind of material.

helpfulResource.displayText: SEC09-BP01 Key and certificate management (AWS Well-Architected)

choices.title: Every expiring material (certificates, CAs, keys, secrets, tokens, IdP metadata, licenses, domains) is inventoried with an owner

helpfulResource.displayText: Good looks like: One inventory lists every material the workload depends on that can expire or be replaced: public and private TLS certificates (including imported and on-host ones), private and cluster certificate authorities, signing and encryption keys, secrets and API keys, third-party and partner tokens, SAML and OIDC identity provider metadata and signing certificates, software licenses and domain registrations. Each entry has an owning team, expiry date, issuer, renewal method and every consumer that must receive the new version. The inventory is generated or reconciled automatically, for example from AWS Certificate Manager, AWS Private CA, AWS Secrets Manager and the IAM credential report, and is reviewed when the architecture changes.

improvementPlan.displayText: Build the inventory from the sources you can query (ACM and AWS Private CA certificates, Secrets Manager secrets, IAM access keys from the credential report, identity provider metadata, registrar and license records) and add the materials you can only find by asking, such as partner-issued tokens and certificates on devices. Assign an owner and a renewal method to each entry, list every consumer, and reconcile the inventory on a schedule and in your deployment pipeline.

content.displayText: Generate credential reports for your AWS account (IAM)
Manage the private CA lifecycle (AWS Private CA)

choices.title: Expiry and renewal-failure alarms fire with a lead time longer than the renewal window

helpfulResource.displayText: Good looks like: Each inventoried material has an alarm that reaches the owning team early enough to renew, distribute and verify by hand if automation fails (for example 30 days or more before a certificate expires, a suggestion), plus an alarm on any failed or stalled renewal. Examples: CloudWatch alarms on the ACM DaysToExpiry metric, EventBridge rules on ACM expiration and renewal-action events, the AWS Config rule acm-certificate-expiration-check, and scheduled checks for materials outside AWS. Imported certificates, which ACM does not renew, are covered. Public certificate lifetimes are shrinking, so expiries come round more often. Platform notes: EC2 and containers: ACM cannot see certificates installed on hosts or in images, so check what each endpoint serves. Kubernetes: include the cluster CA. Serverless and managed endpoints: prefer ACM certificates. Partition notes: ACM, AWS Config and Amazon EventBridge are available in AWS GovCloud (US) as of 2026-10-06; verify per Region.

improvementPlan.displayText: For each kind of material, pick the signal (ACM metric or event, AWS Config rule, or a scheduled check that reads the expiry date from the served certificate, the secret or the registrar), set the lead time longer than your manual renewal and distribution time, and route it to the owning team's paging or ticket queue. Add alarms on renewal failure, test that each alarm fires, and review open expiry alarms in your operations review.

content.displayText: AWS Config managed rule acm-certificate-expiration-check
AWS Certificate Manager FAQs (public certificate validity periods)
How to manage certificate lifecycles using ACM event-driven workflows (AWS Security Blog)

choices.title: No client or component pins a leaf certificate, and any pinning is to a certificate authority

helpfulResource.displayText: Good looks like: No mobile app, device, partner integration, SDK configuration or service pins the leaf certificate of any endpoint, so a routine renewal or replacement cannot break clients. Where a use case requires pinning, it pins to a certificate authority you control or to all the issuing root CAs (for example all Amazon Trust Services root certificates for ACM public certificates), and the pin set can be updated without a client release. Partners that pin are told before CA changes. Reader note: The ORR whitepaper page linked here also mentions AWS Systems Manager Incident Manager, which is closed to new customers; it is not needed for this practice.

improvementPlan.displayText: Search client code, mobile and device builds, SDK configurations and partner integration documents for pinned certificates or public-key hashes. Replace leaf pins with CA or root pins, or remove pinning, ship the change before the next renewal, and add a check to code review and the pipeline that rejects new leaf pins.

choices.title: Renewal and deployment to every consumer are automated wherever the issuer supports it, and rotation has been exercised

helpfulResource.displayText: Good looks like: Certificates renew automatically (ACM managed renewal with DNS validation), secrets and keys rotate on a schedule (Secrets Manager rotation), and new versions reach every consumer automatically, including hosts, containers, partner trust stores and IdP settings. Each rotation was exercised in the last 12 months, including any certificate authority you run. Platform notes: Amazon EKS: rotate the cluster CA with EKS CA rotation, updating the worker nodes you manage and external clients (kubeconfig, CI/CD) before activation. If you do not, EKS appends a successor CA about 2 years before expiry and activates it, so route the AWS Health notices to the owner. Identity: rotate IdP and IAM Identity Center SAML signing certificates. Partition notes: EKS CA rotation covers commercial Regions, and AWS Capabilities by Region does not list it for AWS GovCloud (US) as of 2026-10-06; verify per Region. There, record each cluster CA expiry and plan a replacement cluster well before it.

improvementPlan.displayText: Move certificates to ACM managed renewal with DNS validation where you can, turn on Secrets Manager rotation for secrets, and automate distribution to every consumer. For materials that cannot renew automatically, write a renewal runbook with owners and lead times. Exercise each rotation in pre-production and then in production on a schedule, and record that clients kept working.

questions.title: Incident exercises: game days, tabletops and recovery drills
questions.description: Maximum risk: High (launch-blocking unless remediated or formally accepted). Category: Escalation. Have the people who would respond to a real event proven, through exercises, that your alarms, runbooks, tools, access and escalation paths work together under realistic conditions? Evidence to collect: the exercise calendar and the reports of the last fault-injection game day and the last tabletop exercise (scenario, date, participants, time to detect and mitigate, findings). The tracker that holds the findings. Restore, failover, break-glass, AZ-shift, runbook, customer-communication and provider-escalation drills are scored in their own questions.

helpfulResource.displayText: REL12-BP05 Conduct game days regularly (AWS Well-Architected)

choices.title: On-call engineers mitigated injected failures (such as AZ impairment or dependency loss) with real alarms in the last 12 months

helpfulResource.displayText: Good looks like: In the last 12 months, faults were injected into a production or production-like environment under realistic load (for example AZ impairment, dependency errors or latency, instance or task loss), the workload's own alarms paged the on-call engineers, and they diagnosed and mitigated using the documented runbooks and their normal access, ideally without being told the scenario in advance. Stop conditions on customer-facing alarms bounded the blast radius, and time to detect and to mitigate were recorded. Platform notes: EC2: instance stop or terminate, network disruption and AZ scenarios in AWS FIS. Containers: Amazon ECS task and Amazon EKS pod actions. Serverless: AWS FIS Lambda invocation error and latency actions, or fault flags in your own code. Partition notes: AWS FIS is available in AWS GovCloud (US) as of 2026-10-06, without the experiment schedule and experiment report features; verify scenario and action availability per Region.

improvementPlan.displayText: Pick two or three failure modes from your failure model, such as loss of one AZ and loss of a critical dependency, and build each as an experiment with stop conditions on customer-facing alarms, for example from the AWS FIS scenario library. Run it first in pre-production at production-like load, then in production with a limited blast radius, with the on-call engineer responding as if it were real. Record time to detect and to mitigate, and file every gap as a finding.

choices.title: A tabletop or live exercise rehearsed incident command, stakeholder communications and escalation to AWS and vendors

helpfulResource.displayText: Good looks like: In the last 12 months, a facilitated tabletop or live exercise walked through a realistic event of the workload's own (for example a Regional impairment, a bad deployment or a data corruption) and rehearsed who leads the incident, how responders are assembled, how status reaches stakeholders and customers, when and how to open a case with AWS Support and other providers, and who makes business decisions such as failing over or accepting degraded service. Gaps and decisions were written up in an after-action report. The same exercise can serve as evidence for the communication plan (event_customer_impact) and provider escalation (event_provider_escalation); this statement scores incident command and decision making.

improvementPlan.displayText: Schedule a tabletop exercise with a facilitator, a written scenario and objectives agreed by leadership. Include the incident lead, on-call engineers, communications and support owners and a business decision maker, and walk through detection, escalation, provider engagement, customer communication and recovery decisions. Capture an after-action report and repeat at least once a year (a suggestion) with a different scenario.

choices.title: Exercises engaged the current on-call, escalation contacts and decision makers, not only runbook authors

helpfulResource.displayText: Good looks like: Participants in the last exercises included engineers from the current on-call rotation who did not write the runbooks, the people on the escalation path (incident leads, management, security, dependency owners and any operations partner), and the business owner who would make customer-impacting decisions. Contact details and access were checked live during the exercise, and new on-call engineers take part in an exercise before or soon after joining the rotation.

improvementPlan.displayText: For each exercise, build the participant list from the current on-call schedule and escalation documents rather than from the team that wrote the runbooks, invite the business decision maker and dependency owners, and confirm each person's contact details and access during the exercise. Track who has taken part, and add new on-call engineers to the next exercise.

choices.title: Exercise findings are tracked to closure, and runbooks, alarms and this checklist are updated

helpfulResource.displayText: Good looks like: Every gap found in an exercise (a missing or late alarm, a wrong runbook step, missing access, an unreachable contact, a slow decision) is recorded as an action with an owner and a due date in the same tracker as other operational work, reviewed in a recurring operations review until closed, and reflected in the runbooks, alarms, escalation documents and the answers in this lens. The next exercise checks that the fixes worked.

improvementPlan.displayText: After each exercise, write the findings as actions with owners and due dates in your work tracker (for example AWS Systems Manager OpsCenter or your ticketing system), review open actions in your operations review, update runbooks, alarms and this lens's answers as actions close, and include a check of past findings in the next exercise.

questions.title: Post-incident analysis and learning loop
questions.description: Maximum risk: High (launch-blocking unless remediated or formally accepted). Category: Forensics. After a customer-impacting event or near-miss, do you analyze what happened without blame, fix the contributing factors, and feed what you learned back into this review? Evidence to collect: the post-incident analysis template. The analyses of the last few events or near-misses (or of comparable workloads for a new launch). The corrective-action tracker with owners, due dates and closure rate. Any ORR questions added or changed because of an incident.

helpfulResource.displayText: REL12-BP02 Perform post-incident analysis (AWS Well-Architected)

choices.title: A blameless written analysis (impact, timeline, contributing factors) follows each customer-impacting event or near-miss

helpfulResource.displayText: Good looks like: A documented process says which events need an analysis (every customer-impacting event and significant near-miss), who writes it and by when. Each analysis records customer impact, a timeline with detection, engagement, mitigation and resolution times, recent changes, the contributing factors found by asking why repeatedly, and what would have detected, diagnosed or mitigated the event sooner. It is blameless: it looks for missing mechanisms rather than people to fault, and it is reviewed by people outside the team. Reader note: This page refers to AWS Systems Manager Incident Manager, which is closed to new customers; any post-incident analysis process or tool meets this practice.

improvementPlan.displayText: Adopt a short template (impact, timeline, contributing factors, detection and mitigation questions, actions), define which events and near-misses require it and the deadline, collect timeline data automatically from alarms, deployments and chat logs, and review each analysis in a recurring meeting with someone outside the owning team. Before launch, run the process on an exercise or on an event from a similar workload.

choices.title: Corrective actions have owners and due dates and are tracked to closure in a recurring review

helpfulResource.displayText: Good looks like: Every corrective action from an analysis is recorded in a work tracker with an owner, a due date and a priority that reflects the risk, and open, overdue and recently closed actions are reviewed in a recurring operations review with leadership present. Actions that prevent recurrence are favored over reminders to be careful, and an action closes only when the fix is in production and verified. Reader note: The OPS11-BP02 page linked here refers to AWS Systems Manager Incident Manager, which is closed to new customers; any work tracker meets this practice.

improvementPlan.displayText: Put every corrective action in the same tracker as other engineering work (for example AWS Systems Manager OpsCenter or your ticketing system) with owner, due date and priority, add an overdue-actions view to your weekly operations review, escalate actions that slip, and require evidence that the fix is in production before closing.

choices.title: Each analysis asks whether an ORR question would have prevented the impact, and gaps become new or revised questions

helpfulResource.displayText: Good looks like: The analysis template asks when the workload's last ORR was done, whether any question would have prevented or reduced the impact, and whether a question was answered incorrectly. When the answer reveals a gap, the team writes a new or revised question with guidance, as described in Appendix A of the AWS ORR whitepaper, and adds it to the organization's own add-on lens; related answers in this lens are revisited.

improvementPlan.displayText: Add ORR questions to your analysis template. For each gap, draft a question, guidance and links to the analysis, and add it to your own add-on custom lens, starting from the templates/org-addon-lens.json template in this lens's repository rather than editing this lens, so your questions survive lens upgrades. Re-answer the affected questions in this lens.
